title: Aged care provider underpaid migrant staff by more than $1m
text:
An aged care provider in the ACT and NSW has been ordered to back pay more than $1.3 million to 335 employees, as part of an enforceable undertaking with the Fair Work Ombudsman.

Goodwin Aged Care Services is a registered charity operating retirement living, residential aged care, home care and allied health services.

Goodwin self-reported its non-compliance in July 2024, with the underpayments occurring between July 2018 and March 2025.

One employee is owed $38,760, while the average back payment for each employee was $4,165.

Migrant staff most-affected

Most of Goodwin's affected staff were based in the ACT, according to the Fair Work Ombudsman (FWO), and included nurses, allied health professionals and care managers, along with staff in food, catering staff, cleaning, laundry and planning and admin staff.

For three quarters of those affected, English was their second language, and 10 per cent were visa holders.

Goodwin operates aged care services in ACT and NSW. (Supplied)

"Migrants and visa holders are a priority for the FWO, as they can be vulnerable in the workplace including due to lack of awareness of laws or concerns about speaking up," Fair Work Ombudsman Anna Booth said.

" Importantly, they have the same rights as any other employees in Australia and have protections for their visa if they call out for help. "

She said the aged care sector was a large employer of migrant workers.

Worker agreements focused on non-monetary benefits

The FWO said Goodwin's non-compliance stemmed from sub-standard 'individual flexibility arrangements' (IFAs), which are alternative working terms made to suit both the employee and employer.

IFAs are required to leave staff "better off overall when compared to their award or registered agreement", the FWO said.

In 313 of these agreements, the FWO found the worker was disadvantaged due to the IFA being "over-reliant" on non-monetary benefits.

It also said due to an "incorrect payroll system configuration", 22 additional residential care employees not on IFAs had not been paid penalty rates for early afternoon shifts.

An audit of alternative worker agreements were too reliant on non-monetary benefits for staff. (Supplied)

Goodwin is the latest aged care company to come under fire from the FWO, after investigations earlier this year found 22 organisations owed more than $5.3 million to 3,600 employees.

The FWO said it is currently auditing 30 providers for compliance with the Fair Work Act.

Goodwin Aged Care said it has completed remediation for all affected employees it could contact, with funds for those it couldn't contact transferred to the FWO.

It also said it has worked to strengthen payroll governance and taken measures to prevent future similar issues.

"Goodwin acted promptly to understand their full extent and support affected employees," a spokesperson said.

title: Diamonds name Klau for Constellation Cup squad
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Diamonds netballer Sarah Klau has retained her spot in Australia's Constellation Cup squad after pleading guilty to assault.

Klau was included in the 14-player squad named on Tuesday, less than a week after the goalkeeper was sanctioned by Netball Australia (NA).

The 31-year-old was handed a $5,000 fine and a two-match ban — suspended for 12 months — by the sport's national governing body.

Klau fined after unprecedented assault charge Diamonds defender Sarah Klau is handed a $5,000 fine and a suspended two-game ban after pleading guilty to assault and failing to disclose the incident prior to the Commonwealth Games.

Klau had fronted Downing Centre Court earlier this month, facing a common assault charge.

She had allegedly kicked a security guard in the back outside a pub in Sydney's eastern suburbs when she was denied entry due to being too intoxicated.

The NSW Swifts player had reportedly attended a Sydney Swans AFL match a day after an ongoing leg injury ruled her out of the remainder of the Super Netball season.

Klau, who has represented Australia on 67 occasions since her Diamonds debut in 2019, failed to disclose the matter to NA before the Commonwealth Games in July, resulting in the sanctions.

Sophie Dwyer also retained her spot in the Diamonds squad, looking for a chance to find redemption after missing an after-the-siren shot in the Commonwealth Games semifinal loss to Jamaica.

Constellation Cup First Test: October 18 (Auckland)

Second Test: October 21 (Christchurch)

Third Test: October 25 (Sydney)

Fourth Test: October 28 (Melbourne)

Dwyer was left on the bench in Australia's bronze-medal win over England in Glasgow.

The core of coach Stacey Marinkovich's squad remains the same from the Games, with Jo Weston unavailable for selection.

Jessie Grenvold, Amy Parmenter and Donnell Wallam return to the side after travelling to Glasgow as reserves.

Grenvold is yet to make her Diamonds debut after earning her maiden call-up in May following a breakout season in defence for the Melbourne Mavericks.

The Constellation Cup begins on October 18, with the Diamonds travelling to Auckland to take on the Commonwealth Games champions.

Diamonds squad: Kiera Austin, Courtney Bruce, Sophie Dwyer, Sophie Garbin, Matilda Garrett, Jessie Grenvold, Georgie Horjus, Sarah Klau, Cara Koenen, Kate Moloney, Amy Parmenter, Jamie-Lee Price, Donnell Wallam, Liz Watson

AAP

title: 'How do you get through this?': Parents on the grief of losing a child
text:
When Kerri Westwood's teenage daughter Lauren became unwell during an overseas school trip, the family assumed it was a virus she picked up while travelling.

Kerri says the 15-year-old saw a doctor and felt "better" so continued on her trip. But when she got home, her condition worsened.

"She'd had a bit of tingling in her fingers, she was just sleeping all the time," says Kerri, from Mount Duneed in Victoria.

"We took her to hospital, and they wanted to do an MRI, that was when they discovered a tumour."

Kerri says the family was "blindsided" by a glioblastoma brain cancer diagnosis.

"Doctors told us, 'Don't Google it,'" says the 52-year-old.

"They gave her three to five years to live.

"How do you tell a 15-year-old that they're going straight into palliative care?"

Lauren died in July 2020, 21 months after her diagnosis.

"She was a beautiful, bright light who left this world far too soon," Kerri says.

"That grief isn't something that you get over, we have to learn to live with it for the rest of our lives."

Lauren was 15 when she was diagnosed with glioblastoma. (Supplied)

Losing the sense of natural order

The death of a child at any age is a "profound loss" because it goes against what we think is natural, says Lauren Breen, a grief researcher and psychologist from Curtin University in Western Australia.

"So not only might we lose this very close relationship, but we've lost our understanding of how the world should be or that sense of natural justice," Professor Breen says.

Kathy Packenas, from child bereavement support organisation Ladybird Care Foundation, says research shows that "bereaved parents are at increased risk of depression, anxiety, trauma-related distress and complex grief".

"The death of a child is often described as one of the most devastating experiences that parents can endure," she says.

"Something of this nature can affect every aspect of a person's life, their mental health, relationships, work, their sense of identity."

Ms Packenas says every parent's relationship with their child is unique and so is their grief.

"We find some people want to talk really openly about their grief and others prefer quieter, more behind-the-scenes forms of support," she says.

" Some people reach out straight away after the death and some people reach out many years later; there's no timeline. "

Have you navigated the grief of losing a child? We'd be honoured to hear from you and what helped, if anything. Share with us here.

Leaning on others who understand

Kerri says over the past six years she has learnt that a lot of different feelings can co-exist.

"Sometimes it's sadness, sometimes it's anger, sometimes it's numbness," she says.

"Sometimes it's just completely overwhelming.

" Then there's sometimes where you can laugh and have a good day, but then suddenly you feel guilty for being happy. "

Kerri says she sought help from a counsellor but found that sharing her experience with other parents who had also lost a child has been healing.

For the past 18 months she has been a peer mentor for 57-year-old Tonya Shoobridge, from Brisbane/Meanjin, whose daughter Madeline died in 2024.

The pair were connected through the Ladybird Care Foundation.

Tonya Shoobridge's daughter Madi died unexpectedly in 2024. (Supplied)

"Madi passed on April 1st, just before her 21st birthday," Tonya says.

Despite Madi having cerebral palsy, Tonya says her death was very unexpected and sudden.

"It's the worst crisis to ever find yourself in; I was very confused and scared," she says.

She says anniversaries, birthdays and Christmas are among the hardest times to navigate, which is when she has leaned on Kerri for support.

" I just said to her, 'How the hell do you do this? How do you get me through this?' "

"She said, 'It just sucks, it's awful'.

"If you go to someone who has been there and knows what it feels like physically to lose a child, then that's where you're going to get the most help."

Sign up to the ABC Lifestyle newsletter Get a mid-week boost and receive easy recipes, wellbeing ideas, and home and garden tips in your inbox every Wednesday. You’ll also receive a monthly newsletter of our best recipes.

Talking about her brings joy

Tonya says her journey with grief has focused on building resilience and looking for positives in every day.

"When you don't want to get out of bed and when you think you're never going to stop crying, you have to ask yourself, 'Is this helping me or is it hurting me?'" she says.

"You can answer that pretty easily, 'No, this is hurting.'

"You can journal, you can write letters to your child and try to think of three good things that have happened that day or three beautiful memories that you have."

Supporting someone who's lost a child Women who have lost children talk about continuing in the wake of such grief, and how people stepped up, or stepped away.

Professor Breen says connection to the child and others during the grief process is really important.

"It's perfectly fine and normal to still talk to the child and share stories of them and keep photos of them and their possessions," she says.

"[And] find the people who you do have that connection with and who can be supportive, that can be really helpful."

Tonya has also asked family and friends to donate money to an all-abilities organisation Madi used to be a part of.

"If you do something to honour your child, give to a charity, raise money, it makes you feel good inside," she says.

"And it answers that question for other people, 'How can I help you?'"

"Help me honour her memory by giving to this place."

Kerri says she wants people to not be afraid to say Lauren's name because talking about her daughter brings her joy.

"Lauren would want us to be happy and not to be rolled up in a ball on the floor," she says.

"When Lauren was sick, we spoke about ways that I would be able to give back to people.

"And I feel like working with Ladybird Care is a way that I can give back to [other] families who are grieving."

title: How Nick Daicos won the Brownlow Medal
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Coming into the night, the 2026 Brownlow Medal count held little intrigue about who the winner would be.

Few — if any — in the footballing world thought there was anyone who could seriously challenge Nick Daicos for the award.

But there was still one person who was in shock: Daicos, himself.

"I can't believe I'm the Brownlow medallist to be honest," Daicos said at the award ceremony in Melbourne.

The count was close until about the halfway mark, before Daicos pulled away from the pack as the season progressed.

With his 47 votes last night, Daicos has earned more votes in the last four years than any other player has in any five-year period.

Daicos earned more votes than three entire clubs. He collected 63 per cent of Collingwood's votes for the evening.

He racked up record after record: the most votes in one year, most consecutive games with three votes (six), the most games with three votes (13).

It wasn't just a win, it was domination.

With the win, Daicos joins Tom Mitchell, Gary Ablett Jr and Ben Cousins as father-son selections who have claimed the Brownlow Medal (Jobe Watson's 2012 victory was rescinded).

Daicos time

Plenty has been written about what makes Daicos special.

Coaches and opposition players talk about his elusiveness, vision and ability to make something out of what seems like nothing.

And then there is his competitiveness.

"He hates losing," Magpies great Scott Pendlebury said.

"Especially at table tennis. Whenever we travel on the road, he always tries to get a re-match."

That competitive drive is often what turns good into great, and great into legendary.

But words pale into insignificance compared to watching the best of Daicos in full flight.

Players like Daicos stand out due to the highlights they create.

Teams spend more time trying to get Daicos off balance than any other player in the competition.

It hasn't seemed to have an effect yet.

No matter what teams throw at Daicos, he still has an unerring habit of getting the ball and letting his imagination run wild.

That drive was forged from his early days as a player, often being one of the slightest on the field when he played up in age at both the Greythorn Falcons and the Kew Rovers.

When Daicos moved to Carey Grammar for year 10, he was thrust immediately into the first team to compete in the prestigious APS football competition.

His teammates were no slouches either, with Daicos playing alongside the likes of Noah Anderson and last year's Brownlow medallist, Matt Rowell.

No player in the AFL was more important in getting his team in scoring positions than Daicos was this year.

Daicos thrived at winning the ball when no-one had clear control.

He has an innate ability to track the ball before anyone else, working smarter and not harder.

Daicos also has a scary ability to render his direct opponents as traffic cones.

The Magpies look to get Daicos the ball as much as possible, and he repays them with territory.

Few can match his combination of skill, speed and footy intelligence.

Although Collingwood fell short this year, hopes are higher for 2027 with additional reinforcements.

Family zone

Throughout football's history, geography has shaped the make-up of teams to a great extent.

Teams recruited from specific regions. The fortunes of clubs rose and fell based on the growth of different geographic areas.

Urban expansion fuelled Hawthorn's rise, while weak and depopulating zones condemned other clubs to near extinction.

There was one exception to the geography-based dictation of the footy landscape: the sons of former players.

The father-son rule was introduced in 1949 to ensure players such as Ron Barassi could continue on the legacy of their fathers at their clubs regardless of geography.

These days, the role of geography has inverted and it now dictates where all the father-son selections are.

The family zone for Victorian footy now runs through south-east Melbourne.

This was the former recruiting area for Hawthorn, otherwise known as the Family Club.

The ranks of father-son selections are littered with schools and clubs based in the most desirable parts of Melbourne, often far from the origins of their fathers' careers.

For example, the Silvangi and Daicos offspring played their junior footy at the Greythorn Falcons.

That's only a stone's throw from Collingwood captain Darcy Moore's junior club of Ivanhoe.

Nor is it far from where Mitchell or Watson first honed their craft.

The eastern side of Melbourne has increasingly become a powerhouse in junior footy as well, with Sandringham, Oakleigh and the Eastern Ranges dominating the AFL's Talent League in recent seasons.

Brownlow's changing face

A major change took place to the fabric of the Brownlow Medal this year.

Umpires gained access to a select group of 17 statistics before voting. Daicos excelled in several of these measures.

This may rob part of what made the Brownlow so special.

Umpires have a unique perspective. They're also party to the intangibles, such as on-field demeanour, respect and sportsmanship.

This year's votes aligned more closely to the results of the AFL Coaches Association award than ever before, according to Wheelo Ratings.

Coaches pore over key numbers throughout their games and now umpires can rely on some of the same figures to adjudge best afield as well.

Supplying data may condition umpires to discard insights gleaned in the heat of the action, turning them instead into just another spin on the same cold distant observations.

Defenders are already suffering even more than they traditionally do, while midfielders, who often accumulate high "count" stats, get a larger share of the spoils.

Rucks also outperformed their expected output this year, likely benefiting from the inclusion of hit-outs.

This will likely serve to further intensify a growing trend towards vote concentration in disposal-accumulating midfielders.

The leaderboard for career-long average votes is strewn liberally with current players, with previous leaders Haydn Bunton and Graham Moss only playing the prime vote-earning part of their careers in the VFL.

If this trend continues, Daicos will soon break Patrick Dangerfield and Ablett Jr's record for most career votes, at least until the next star enters the scene.

But all of that is for the future.

All that is important now is that the inevitable ascension of Daicos to the pinnacle of the game has taken place.

title: WA introduces nation's 'most comprehensive ban' on smart glasses in schools
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Western Australia will introduce the nation's strictest ban on smart glasses in public schools, the state's education minister has announced.

The devices, which look like ordinary glasses, allow the wearer to capture images, video and audio with the press of a button, and have attracted the nickname "pervert glasses" because it is not always clear when they are in use.

Education Minister Sabine Winton said students, staff, parents, carers and even contractors would be forbidden from wearing or storing the devices on school premises under the nation's "most comprehensive" ban.

Sabine Winton has announced a ban on smart glasses in all WA state schools. (ABC News: Kenith Png)

The new rules, which will take effect at the start of term 4, will also apply to any offsite location where students and staff are representing their school, such as sports events and excursions.

"Smart glasses may look cool but there's absolutely no place in our schools or classrooms for them," she said.

"We know the devices are becoming increasingly popular and increasingly accessible and cheap and there is a growing community concern about the risk of careless, criminal and malicious activity."

Push for nationally consistent laws

Every state and territory has some form of restriction on personal mobile phones and devices, with some, including WA, banning their use during school hours.

Labor AI rules Smart glasses could be prohibited in Commonwealth workplaces as the government consults on new rules for Australia's growing AI sector.

The South Australian Greens are pushing for a statewide ban on smart glasses from places like schools, gyms and swimming pools.

In response, South Australian Deputy Premier and Attorney-General Kyam Maher said he would seek advice from his department on the adequacy of current state laws.

He was also in discussions with the federal attorney-general about coming up with a plan for national consistent laws.

In Victoria, "wearable devices" like smartwatches and smart glasses are not currently banned in schools but will be from January 2027.

Ms Winton said WA was going "a step further" than other states, because it would be the first to entirely ban the possession of smart glasses by anyone who stepped foot on school grounds.

'Preventative action'

The minister urged private and independent schools to also ban the devices.

She said principals would be able to grant exemptions for students with special needs or medical conditions.

Ms Winton said the education department had not recorded any instances of smart glasses being used "irresponsibly" in schools, and said prevention was the key driver behind the ban.

Cheap smart glasses shockingly hackable Independent testing finds a hacker can access cheap smart glasses without a password.

"I just think it is a really important stance to take before this gets ahead of us," she said.

"We know these devices are becoming increasingly popular with kids … this is a preventive action to make sure that school principals can get on with their important role in leading their schools, and making sure that teachers can teach."

There is growing support for a ban on the import of low-cost devices that are being used to film people without their consent.

Do you know more? Contact Callum Liddelow.

An ABC investigation found the devices were exposing Australians' sensitive data, images and videos to hackers.

It comes after the City of Vincent last week instructed its chief executive officer to prepare a report for the council to consider the privacy and safety concerns stemming from the use of smart glasses in city-owned facilities, including recreational centres and libraries.

The report will consider whether the Perth council's existing laws, which ban the use of devices to record someone without their consent at a community facility, are sufficient, and whether it is necessary to beef up enforcement powers.

title: Giving birth among 'flies and trucks' becoming more common in parts of NSW
text:
Tell us about your experience.

When Shara Kimpton gave birth to her third child five weeks early in 2023, she was in a rest area on the Sturt Highway in the New South Wales Riverina region.

She and her mother had been on their way to the Griffith Hospital, more than 90 kilometres from home, but the baby was in no mood to wait.

"It was quite the rush and everything was a blur," Ms Kimpton said.

"But I just had to follow my instincts because that was the only thing I had.

"There was lots of flies and trucks going past … out in the elements."

Shara Kimpton says she was forced to give birth among flies and with trucks going past. (Supplied: Shara Kimpton)

Stories like Ms Kimpton's are becoming more common.

Twenty-five years ago, the rate of babies being born before arriving at hospital in NSW was similar whether you lived in a regional or a metropolitan area.

But that figure has long been diverging, with rates since doubling in regional local health districts.

In outer regional and remote areas, it has more than tripled.

Rates are highest on the Central Coast and northern NSW, where one in 67 babies is now born before making it to hospital.

Do you know more about this or have a similar story? Email pezet.lauren@abc.net.au or laurenpezet@proton.me

The NSW Health data includes:

planned homebirths before a midwife arrived

freebirths, which is distinct from a homebirth and occurs without a registered midwife or doctor present, before a hospital presentation

births at home or in transit before a planned hospital birth

There is no breakdown of those categories.

Perinatal social worker and regional maternity advocate Jen Laurie said anecdotally many were those in transit, known as "roadside births".

Ms Laurie has spoken to dozens of women about their birthing experience and through her Bush Babies campaign, lobbying the NSW government, with many sharing stories of births at rest stops and in toilet blocks.

"I sometimes wonder if it's going to take a catastrophic outcome for somebody to be really creative and start listening and do something about it," she said

Jen Laurie says the regional maternity system is a "networked mess". (ABC News: Peter Sanders)

NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said he wanted to "get that number down" and would consider a target if it was advised by the recently appointed inaugural chief midwife.

"It is still small as a percentage of all births, but every time that happens, it causes concern, particularly for mums and families," he said.

Ms Kimpton said despite her history of quick deliveries, when she fell pregnant again with her fourth child she was not offered an appointment with her local clinic until about halfway through her pregnancy, and was not given any alternative options other than driving in for the delivery.

Homebirth was not an option available to her so she planned to freebirth at home despite the known risks, which can include undetected complications, and then present to hospital as she did not want to risk giving birth on the side of the road again.

"Our only option is go to your closest local midwifery-included hospital or even further, pretty much for centralised care," she said.

Shara Kimpton opted to give birth to her fourth child at home, fearing another roadside birth. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

In a statement, Murrumbidgee Local Health District apologised that Griffith Hospital was not able to provide Ms Kimpton with an antenatal visit before the recommended 14 weeks, and that maternity staff aimed to provide ongoing support and information for birth and emergency options.

"We continue to listen to and learn from women about their experiences to help us plan and improve the care provided within our maternity services to meet the needs of the local community," the statement said.

Ms Kimpton said if Hay, the closest town to her property, still had a birthing option like it used to, she could have planned to go there instead.

The birth certificate for Shara Kimpton's son shows he was born at "Birdcage Rest Area". (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Birthing options centralised

Ms Laurie said she felt the reason behind the increase was clear.

"The reduction of services and the centralisation of services," she said.

"A lot of these regional rural remote places that are no longer offering birthing previously did."

Dozens of birthing services have closed or been suspended under both Labor and Coalition governments across NSW over recent decades.

Examples of mothballed maternity units include the unit at Parkes, which has lay dormant since 2019 because not enough staff want to work there, but Ryan Park said he was still working towards opening it.

The barely used birthing suite in Parkes remains closed due to a lack of available staff. (ABC Central West: Xanthe Gregory)

There was also Muswellbrook, which closed in 2022, forcing expectant mothers to travel 100km to Maitland.

The Upper Hunter Shire Council has expressed fears Scone could be in a similar situation when its only obstetrician retires at the end of 2026, with recruitment still underway.

The closure of the maternity ward at Yass in 2004 has seen women give birth on the Barton Highway on the way to Canberra.

In Tumut, birthing has been suspended after its only obstetrician was banned from practising at the hospital, with women being sent more than 100km away to Wagga Wagga until the position is filled.

Mr Park acknowledged there had been a "change in the midwifery model" over time with a "focus on safety", which he said also had challenges.

"It has to be a service that operates around the clock, and that's why governments of all persuasions probably over the last 25 years have concentrated those services around major hubs and major hospitals," he said.

"What we've tried to do, and our approach is slightly different, we're trying to get more women to be able to birth as close to where they live as possible.

"We've expanded homebirthing and we've expanded midwifery group practices."

Ryan Park says he wants to see more birthing options closer to home, while balancing resourcing challenges. (ABC News: Billy Cooper)

There is strict criteria around location and pregnancy risk for women wanting a homebirth, and midwifery group practices generally provide antenatal and postnatal care.

Mr Park also said more than 300 new midwifery places had been filled since 2023, with half of those in rural and regional areas.

He said there was "more work to do".

" I've made it clear to the department I want the focus on trying to open up these birthing services, but I've got to balance that out with making sure that we've got the staff in place. "

A statewide maternity service plan is also due at the end of the year.

Midwives working in 'pressure cooker'

On the Central Coast, the measured impact of the closure of a private maternity unit last year is not clear as the data only goes up to 2024.

Gosford-based doula and educator Gemma Wilson said with Wyong's maternity ward also closed since 2020, the situation on the Central Coast was "dire".

There is currently only one maternity ward to cater for more than 3,500 births each year.

Gemma Wilson is a doula and educator based in Gosford. (ABC News: Tamara Penniket)

"It's been a bit of a snowball effect that's continued to happen here," she said.

" [Midwives are] trying to provide the best care and do the best that they can, but they are literally working in a pressure cooker right now in that system. "

Ms Wilson said while the federal government had allocated $10 million to provide additional support to Gosford's remaining maternity ward, there had not been much improvement.

Gosford Hospital has the only remaining maternity ward on the Central Coast. (ABC News: Tamar Penniket)

She also said while a publicly funded homebirth service opened on the Central Coast in 2023, it did not counter the impact of losing Wyong's birth centre.

"We have nowhere for women in the north end of the coast to birth at," she said.

NSW Health said while there had been a small increase in the number of women giving birth at Gosford Hospital since Gosford Private closed its ward, it was not as much as predicted.

Broader impact

Tim McEwen from the Australian Paramedics Association (NSW) said the data showing an increase in births before arrivals correlates with what paramedics see on the ground.

He also thought a reduction in services was behind the trend.

"In a lot of regional towns there's only one ambulance on duty, and that ambulance may not be in town at the time of the medical emergency," Mr McEwen said.

" So the potential for having no maternity unit and no ambulance or backup ambulance available is really quite a frightening prospect both for the public and us as paramedics. "

In a statement, NSW Health said local health districts were focused on filling midwifery and obstetric vacancies through targeted workforce planning, university partnerships, internal pathway programs and tertiary study subsidies.

"We strongly encourage all pregnant women to consult with registered healthcare providers early in their pregnancy, for personalised advice about the best options for themselves and their baby, including options for pregnancy care and birth location," the statement said.

title: Council says there's 'no land' for charity's request for rough sleepers
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The head of a food charity in far-west New South Wales has been left frustrated after being told there was no council land available to build a homeless camp.

Feeding Friends had asked Broken Hill City Council for a block of council land or an unused building to establish a base for homelessness services, including a food outlet, laundry facilities and a transitional camp.

Broken Hill City Council has indicated no land is available to build a camp for those experiencing homelessness. (ABC News: Declan Gooch)

The charity said it was responding to an "urgent need for secure, stable spaces" in the mining city, where those experiencing homelessness could set up temporary and safe shelters.

While the council voted to investigate whether any land was available, Mayor Tom Kennedy made it clear there was not.

"Initial findings is there is no land," Mr Kennedy said.

"So for Feeding Friends to go any further, they're going to have to acquire land themselves.

"[But] what's been proposed before council requires significant planning … [and] vast public consultation."

Prior to the meeting to discuss the request, some locals raised concerns over the encampment's impact on neighbouring residents and businesses.

Tom Kennedy says extensive public consultation and planning approvals would be needed for a homeless encampment. (ABC Broken Hill: Kristina Rosengren)

Demand is increasing

After five years serving hot meals to those experiencing homelessness in Broken Hill, Feeding Friends president Don Barron said demand for its services were growing amid the cost-of-living crisis.

He said the charity now needed a permanent location for its food services.

"I was very disappointed [land wasn't available]," Mr Barron said.

Don Barron says all levels of government need to come together to address homelessness. (ABC Broken Hill: Bill Ormonde)

"[The need] has certainly grown in the way of young families.

"We have homeless people in Broken Hill that do have children, they still go to school but they're living in cars.

"It's probably a lack of housing which is the main reason why people are living in cars … [also] affordability, the cost of living is just gone out of control."

No 'legal framework' to address homelessness

Derwent Coshott, a senior lecturer in law at Sydney University, said legally establishing a transitional campsite would require planning approvals.

But he said there was another pathway through a policy of non-enforcement, referring to the state government's protocol for homeless people in public places.

"The policies that have been adopted have been permissive, in so far as you kind of just let people camp there and you don't enforce the law to move them on," Dr Coshott said.

Derwent Coshott says there is no proper legal framework to address homelessness in these circumstances. (Supplied: Dr Derwent Coshott)

Feeding Friends could ask the council to not enforce the law against them, he said.

"The risk is, of course, that none of this means that the law might not be enforced against them later on."

However, Dr Coshott said the issue raised broader questions about regulating homelessness in NSW.

"We have a NSW administrative protocol that's effectively saying, 'Look, we don't actually have a law that properly deals with this, so the way we're going to deal with this is by not enforcing the law'," Dr Coshott said.

" That basically tells you where the problem is, in the sense that there is no real proper legal framework to address homelessness in these circumstances. "

For Mr Barron, who knows what it's like to sleep rough, it is about confronting homelessness head-on.

"It's not just local council's problem, it's a three-tier problem — local council, which doesn't have funds to do it, the state government, which does, and the federal government, which does," Mr Barron said.

"We all need to sit down as a three-tier society, and involve the public, of how we can address this issue."

title: Coalition weighing options to use super to boost home ownership
text:
Shadow Housing Minister Andrew Bragg has again entered the political fray over super, re-litigating the argument that the retirement savings scheme should be used to help people buy a home — but has stopped short of announcing any policies.

While some of his colleagues support the discussion, Opposition Leader Angus Taylor stressed that no policy decisions had been made.

"We'll say more about housing policy more generally over the next little while," Mr Taylor said.

Senator Bragg will give a speech later today where he is expected to float ideas about how super could be used to boost home ownership ahead of retirement.

"We don't want to become a nation where renting in retirement becomes mandatory," Senator Bragg told ABC News Radio on Tuesday.

" We want to have a country where people can live in their own house … if their superannuation can help them do that, then we should look at that. "

Senator Bragg will argue in his speech that, in retirement, Australians are best served by owning a residence as a top priority, and second, owning financial assets to draw an income or replace the pension in old age.

Policy ideas floated

Senator Bragg said the Coalition had canvassed multiple options, including using super as collateral for a loan or withdrawing a lump sum for a house deposit.

But he said he was not advocating for any particular solutions for now, ahead of a speech he will give at the Financial Services Council later today.

"You could keep the money in the system, and it could operate as a collateral or an offset," he told ABC News Radio.

"You could take it out to pay off a mortgage or to pull together a first home loan."

The Coalition's policy at the last two elections was to allow people to withdraw $50,000 from their super to put towards a house deposit.

Opposition leader Angus Taylor said that was no longer the Coalition's stance.

"It's not Coalition policy," he told reporters on Tuesday.

When asked about Senator Bragg's idea of using super to increase a person's borrowing capacity, he didn't engage with the idea.

"Superannuation is Australians' money … They should have a choice in it. That's why we strongly support self-managed super funds," Mr Taylor said.

" But the proposal you're talking about there is not our policy. "

Where does super go when you die? Millions of Australians could have no say in who inherits their super. Here's how to check if you're one of them.

Senator Bragg admitted a "credible critique" of the former policy was that it was more likely for people in their mid to late 30s who would have accrued $50,000 in super, and therefore the policy would not have significantly helped younger people.

While stressing that the Coalition had not settled on its formal policy, Senator Bragg insisted there was a need to look at different ways super could be used to help people buy their first home.

"I think most people would want their well-paid politicians to be pushing out the boat on some ideas that might be able to help them achieve their goal of home ownership," he said.

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson said those ideas were "a welcome part of the conversation".

"The biggest leading indicator of poverty in retirement is people don't own their own home," he said.

"This is why home ownership is so important, and we need it to take precedence as the primary economic interest for retirement and during your working life."

Shadow Treasurer Tim Wilson says the government needs to prioritise housing. (ABC News: Brendan Esposito)

Nationals leader Matt Canavan said Senator Bragg was a "thought leader" and that the Coalition was formulating its policies ahead of the next election.

"Generally speaking, of course, it's our policy that people should have a choice when it comes to how they use their superannuation," he said.

Debate heats up on super

Superannuation has become a political flashpoint in recent weeks, with One Nation releasing a policy that would allow people to divert funds from their super to pay their rent or mortgage.

That policy would allow people to keep 3 per cent of their salary that would otherwise go to super for a three-year period, which would be $2,300 per year (or $44 per week) for a person on a $90,500 salary.

Some critics have said the measure could be inflationary in the short term and would impact the compound-interest growth of super savings in the long term.

Labor slammed the One Nation policy and has declared the next election will be a "referendum" on superannuation — a key creation of the Labor Keating government in the 1990s.

Under the government's first home super saver scheme, first introduced by a Coalition government, people can make voluntary contributions to their super, let it accrue interest, and later withdraw up to $50,000 as part of a home deposit.

Treasurer Jim Chalmers says the Coalition and One Nation "hate super". (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the Coalition and One Nation were "coming after super", and they wanted to "vandalise" the retirement savings scheme.

"They hate super. They always have and they always will," Mr Chalmers told ABC Radio National on Tuesday.

"That would be devastating for people's retirement incomes. It would make people worse off.

title: The mill 200 farmers can't afford to lose
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The country's last grower-owned sugar mill is seeking a multi-million-dollar loan from the Queensland government to keep it afloat.

Isis Central Sugar Mill, four hours north of Brisbane, has been crushing cane for 129 years.

It employs 250 people during the on-season and supports more than 1,500 jobs across the supply chain.

Isis Central Sugar Mill has been operating for almost 130 years. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

The 2026 season has been plagued by mechanical issues, including one of the mill's two boilers being offline for five weeks, reducing the crushing rate.

The mill is aiming to crush just under 1.2 million tonnes this year, but is 51,000 tonnes behind schedule two months out from the end of the season.

Isis Central Sugar Mill chief executive Simon Brooks said work stoppages contributed to the financial strain, but most of the pressure was due to global market conditions.

"We're absolutely dependent on the sugar pricing for our revenue and, where you see a reduction in that sugar pricing, you have a corresponding reduction on your bottom line," Mr Brooks said.

Simon Brooks wants the federal government to match any state funding. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

The mill's board said it had reached an in-principle agreement with the state government for a loan capped at $9 million.

The money is expected to cover expenses until September 2027, just before the end of the annual crush.

Mr Brooks wants the federal government to match the state funding, noting a promising business case for a bioenergy precinct adjacent to the mill.

"$18 million would go a long way to providing security," he said.

"The business strategy is to diversify.

"We will still be a mill at the end of the day, but there's so much more we can do to make ourselves less dependent on pure sugar output, and that's doing more with assets that we have."

The mill supports about 1,700 jobs. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

'Our only option'

About 200 growers, from the Fraser Coast through to the North Burnett, supply cane to Isis Central Sugar Mill.

Throughput at Isis increased 50 per cent when it started accepting cane from the Maryborough district following the closure of the town's local mill in 2020.

Maryborough Canegrowers chair Roger Bambling said it would be devastating to endure another mill closure.

"It would leave a big hole," he said.

"The whole secret is just to keep talking to each other, the mill and the growers. We're all in it together."

Roger Bambling says the mill is the last hope for Maryborough farmers after their local mill closed. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

In addition to the sugar prices and maintenance costs, transport accounts for a large portion of the mill's rising expenses.

About 100 truck trips are needed each day to transport cane from Maryborough to rail transfer stations bound for the mill.

"Road freight is expensive, and we're looking at how to better manage that," Mr Brooks said.

Conditions to crush

Queensland Minister for Primary Industries Tony Perrett confirmed discussions were underway.

Details of the state government's potential $9 million loan were still being finalised, but it was expected to come with a three-year term, and repayments could include a grower-paid levy.

Farmers said they were happy to pay any potential levies but feared there was not enough certainty.

Tony Russo says sugarcane is the backbone of the Childers community. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

Third-generation canegrower Tony Russo had started planting for next year's crop, cautiously planning for future seasons.

"Everybody's concerned, but a lot of people have got that positive mindset that we've got to still grow and present as much cane as we can because, if we start not growing the cane and not putting the fertiliser on and not watering, then we don't have tonnes and we have more of a problem," Mr Russo said.

It is a fight canefarmers throughout Queensland know all too well.

Mossman Mill in Far North Queensland went into voluntary administration in 2023 after receiving nearly $48 million in state and federal assistance.

On the Gold Coast, about 50 growers who supply Rocky Point Sugar Mill will lose their cane supply agreements after 2027. The state government is working to support affected farmers.

Growers are rushing to harvest the last of their cane ahead of the mid-November crush finish. (ABC News: Tayla Larsen)

Mr Russo hoped Isis Central Sugar Mill's partnerships and progress on biofuels could be enough to get governments on board.

"Everybody's talking about bioenergy, jet aviation fuel, so there is some light at the end of the tunnel," he said.

"We're just on a bit of a tricky path right now."

Assistant Minister for Agriculture, Fisheries and Forestry Anthony Chisholm said the federal government was engaging with operators of the mill.

"We understand the importance of the Isis Central Sugar Mill to its workforce and the region's canegrowers," he said.

title: One Nation wants environmental water 'unlocked' for agriculture this season
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Irrigators and One Nation are calling for environmental water in the Murray-Darling Basin to be made available for agricultural production this season.

The Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder manages a portfolio of more than 3,200 gigalitres of water to improve the health of the basin.

Australia's largest rice processor SunRice laid off 80 workers last month in response to low crop production and the company has asked the federal government to consider making some of that water available for sale to irrigators this summer.

SunRice has laid off 80 works at mills in Leeton and Deniliquin. (ABC News: Emily Doak)

Farrer MP David Farley, of One Nation, introduced a motion to federal parliament last week proposing allocating 75 per cent of available environmental water to irrigators through a "transparent and market-based process".

He has asked the government to respond by early October ahead of the summer crop planting season.

"Miss it and our regional economies contract for another year, catch it and they respond immediately," he told the parliament.

" The land is ready, our farmers are skilled, the equipment is in the paddocks, and our forward markets are already pricing Australian-grown food. "

Plan dismissed by government and conservationists

The Commonwealth Environmental Water Holder, Simon Banks, said the entitlements purchased by the government were subject to the same allocation rules as those held by irrigators.

"When there's less water, against entitlements, which happens in dry periods, we have typically less water available as well," he said.

" My primary responsibility is … protecting and restoring the rivers, wetlands and flood plains of the Murray-Darling Basin. "

Federal Water Minister Murray Watt was not available for interview but in a statement said, "Our policy ensures water is sold fairly and without bias, when and where it won't harm the environment, rather than just picking winners."

Craig Wilkins says water is needed to support environmental outcomes in the basin this summer. (ABC News)

Murray-Darling Conservation Alliance co-director Craig Wilkins said there would be a cost if water set aside for the environment was made available for irrigation.

"We reject this idea that somehow the environmental water is just sitting there doing nothing," he said.

"It needs to be available for this concerning trend around El Niño for this summer, we've got impacts like bird flu … so we need to get more water onto wetlands to protect our bird life."

Rain boosts water allocations

The Australian Bureau of Agricultural and Resource Economics and Sciences crop report for September is forecasting rice production will fall by another 22 per cent, while cotton planting is also expected to be down by a third because of the dry season.

This summer's rice crop is expected to fall by another 22 per cent to 130,000 tonnes. (ABC Riverina: Shannon Corvo)

Recent rain has brought some relief for irrigators in southern NSW.

The water allocation for general security licence holders has increased by 10 per cent for the NSW Murray Valley to 28 per cent of entitlement.

In the Murrumbidgee Valley there has been a 7 per cent rise to 41 per cent of entitlement.

Brian Martin enjoys growing rice on his Burraboi farm. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Burraboi farmers Brian and Alex Martin have set aside 60 hectares to grow rice this year.

"There's something about going around your rice water in the heat of the day with a beer and cruising around checking it," Mr Martin said.

" It's probably the most valuable crop that we grow. "

It is estimated that since water buybacks have been introduced, half of the irrigated farmland in the Edward Kolety-Wakool region is no longer used for irrigation.

Mr Martin said that had a big impact on the community

"All the towns have seen a decrease … the news agency for the amount of papers they sell, how many beers the pub pours a week, it just snowballs to every aspect of every community around it," he said.

"Unless they [governments] want to stay out of the water buybacks or sell some water back to us, you'll see a trend, definite trend in the price of food and cost of production."

Noel Baxter is planting cotton and maize. (ABC News: Kyle Harley)

Berrigan district farmer Noel Baxter will not be using his increased water allocation to grow rice, instead he is planting cotton and maize.

"We haven't grown rice for about 25 years," he said.

"Rice is a great crop and a good industry, but water has become very scarce and expensive and it uses more water than alternative crops and the margins on it just don't stack up."

Mr Baxter said uncertainty around water availability also meant many growers were no longer planting summer crops.

title: 13yo Mount Isa bull rider sets sights on Texas
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Inside the Kalkadoon Arena, in the heart of Queensland's wild north-west, courage can be measured in eight seconds.

The Mount Isa Rodeo is the biggest in the Southern Hemisphere and this year some of its youngest riders made the biggest impression.

Kalkadoon and Pitta Pitta cowgirl Lareece Daley-Kennedy, 13, is preparing to step onto the international stage after receiving invitations to two youth world finals in the United States.

Bull riding runs in the family for Lareece Daly-Kennedy, who took up the sport after hearing stories about her dad's rodeo days. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

She has been invited to compete at the Professional Youth Roughstock Association World Finals in Oklahoma and the World Championship Mini Bulls World Finals in Texas.

The invitations follow a string of strong performances across the North West, including a second-place finish on her first steer ride earlier this year.

At this year's Mount Isa Rodeo she came just short of the buzzer in the Mount Isa round before returning to place third in the Indigenous mini bulls.

Lareece Daley-Kennedy prepares to ride at the Mount Isa Rodeo. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Now the Mount Isa Rodeo is putting real weight behind that next generation, committing $10,000 to help get Lareece to the United States.

It is the first time the incumbent board has directly backed a young rider in this way.

For Lareece, the secret to lasting eight seconds is simple.

"Just lock your knees in and your legs and just hold on," she said.

Lareece was not the only young rider to impress.

Cloncurry brothers Dallas and Ashley Murphy, aged 10 and 14, swept the mini bull titles.

Cloncurry brothers Dallas (10) and Ashley (14) Murphy won the mini bull titles. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Cade Ferguson, 19, was crowned the rodeo's all-round cowboy, just weeks after becoming world champion in bull riding and reserve world champion in saddle bronc at the Cinch World Championship Junior Rodeo in Oklahoma.

Cloncurry's Cade Ferguson (19) was crowned the Mount Isa Rodeo’s all-round cowboy. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

In her father's footsteps

Lareece took up riding after hearing stories about her father Nathan Kennedy's own days in the sport.

"I just wanted to follow my dad's footsteps," she said.

Lareece Daley-Kennedy embraces her father Nathan Kennedy after coming third at the Mount Isa Rodeo. (Supplied: Mount Isa Mines Rodeo )

The sport has taught her how to take a hard landing and get back up.

Earlier this year she was winded on her first steer ride and last year at Cloncurry she was thrown and landed on her neck.

"I'd heard people say, 'Oh, she came second', and I just got up like nothing happened," she said.

Her family initially set out to raise about $15,000 to make the trip to the US possible, with supporters across the north-west chipping in through raffles and donations.

Then came the call from the Mount Isa Rodeo to the shock and delight of her family.

"Blew me away, made me cry actually," Mr Kennedy said.

"It's got us there. It's got us over the line."

Backing the young ones

The junior clinic teaches young riders safety, technique and competition skills. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

The Mount Isa Rodeo has already had to fight for its own future.

The event fell into voluntary administration in September 2024, before a group of residents rallied to revive it for last year, bringing it back before a record crowd.

Now the board is turning its attention to the riders coming through.

Mount Isa Rodeo vice-chair Marcus Curr said developing young riders was becoming an important part of the organisation's future.

Marcus Curr says supporting young riders is an important part of the rodeo's future. (Supplied: Marcus Curr)

"A lot of kids in the bush … don't get to play cricket and football as much as city kids do," he said.

"So rodeo is a big part of their life and their culture."

The board runs an annual junior clinic where young people including children from remote communities learn about safety, technique and competition.

Young riders learn early that rodeo takes courage — and knowing how to get back up. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Mr Curr estimated about 50 children attended this year.

Smaller rodeos across the region also give young competitors somewhere to build their skills before stepping into the Kalkadoon Arena.

Mr Curr said the Murphy brothers and Cade Ferguson were examples of what can happen when talent was matched with family support and opportunities to compete.

"If there's talent around, we've got to support them and encourage them and give them opportunities," he said.

About 50 riders took part in this year’s junior clinic. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

Beyond the Kalkadoon Arena

Mr Curr said he wanted the Mount Isa Rodeo to become "more than just running a rodeo for the weekend".

Young riders are being given opportunities to develop their skills. (Supplied: Pete Wallis)

"It's about investing in opportunities for kids and having Mount Isa Rodeo being a part of Australia developing some of the best cowboys and cowgirls in the world," he said.

For Lareece, one of those opportunities is already waiting in the United States, with plenty of pressure and expectation.

But ask what she loves most about bull riding and the answer is much simpler.

" Winning and holding on. "

Advance Metals’ recent diamond core drilling has bored through a bonanza-grade one-metre intercept grading an eye-watering 4120 grams per tonne (g/t) silver at its flagship Gavilanes project in Mexico. The result came from just 66.7m depth downhole and formed part of a broader 4.6-metre intercept assaying an impressive 945g/t silver, 1.4 per cent zinc and one per cent lead. The result represents the highest ever individual silver assay returned from Advance’s drilling program at Gavilanes. The hole was designed to test for extensions below a high-grade hit in a recently drilled diamond hole and has successfully extended mineralisation, which remains open at depth and to the southwest. Cut diamond drill core from the headline hole, from 102.7 to 103.0m downhole depth, showing semi-massive coarse-grained lead sulphide (grey), with zinc sulphide (pale yellow), minor copper sulphide (bright yellow) and quartz (white). Adding another layer of potential value, the same hole also delivered the project’s most significant high-grade zinc-lead intersection encountered to date. A deeper 12-metre zone from 98.5m assayed 21g/t silver, 3.8 per cent zinc and 3.7 per cent lead. The interval also included a richer 5.3-metre core going 36g/t silver, 7.7 per cent zinc and 6.3 per cent lead from 102.7m. The results point to an expanding polymetallic system at Gavilanes, which lies just 23 kilometres from First Majestic Silver’s world-class San Dimas mine in Mexico’s silver-rich Sierra Madre Occidental Volcanic Belt. That operation has so far produced a massive 745 million ounces of silver and 11 million ounces of gold.

Advertisement

‘The drilling to date has identified high grade silver together with gold, copper, zinc and lead mineralisation.’ Advance Metals managing director and chief executive officer Dr Adam McKinnon First Majestic’s 2024 technical report on its resource and reserve estimates identified more than 125 mineralised quartz veins across its San Dimas property, with the silver and gold-rich quartz veins traced underground for strike lengths ranging from just a few metres to more than 1.5 kilometres. Advance Metals managing director and chief executive officer Dr Adam McKinnon said: “At over 4,000g/t silver, GV-26-008 returned the highest individual silver assay grade in Advance’s program to date and one of the best recorded at the project. The hole also returned the highest grade zinc-lead interval encountered at the Project to date, including 5.3 metres at 14% Zn+Pb - highlighting the potential for significant base metal credits as the mineralised footprint grows.” While silver remains the headline act, recent drilling to the south has also started to outline gold-dominant potential. Three drill holes have all returned gold-focused intersections, with a best result of 2.4m at 2.0g/t gold, 21g/t silver, 1.2 per cent zinc and 2.2 per cent lead from a shallow 14.4m. The company’s latest successes appear well timed, with Mexico’s long-running mining permitting logjam finally beginning to loosen under President Claudia Sheinbaum.

Advertisement

According to Mexican mining industry body CAMIMEX, the country’s Economy Ministry has now cleared more than 90 per cent of the mining permits within its remit, while environmental authority Semarnat has approved more than 85 per cent of its backlog. The shift is significant for a sector that only last month estimated some US$11 billion (A$15.5 billion) of potential mining investment was being held up by outstanding approvals. There is, however, an important wrinkle in Mexico’s improving regulatory story. While the permitting door is swinging open for companies that already hold mining concessions, securing brand-new exploration ground remains another matter. Mexico stopped granting new concessions in 2019 and the Sheinbaum administration has continued to take a cautious approach to opening fresh ground. The change therefore looks more like a controlled thaw than a wholesale reopening of Mexico’s mining sector, with the government clearing bureaucratic bottlenecks around existing projects while retaining tighter control over new concessions. Not that the distinction should trouble Advance at its key Mexican projects. Its Gavilanes project already comprises 11 mining concessions covering 136 square kilometres and a further seven concessions at its 100%-owned Yoquivo silver project in Chihuahua, all in good standing. Advance’s maiden drilling program at its 136-square-kilometre project is squarely aimed at growing and converting the project’s existing foreign resource estimate of 2.83 million tonnes at 246g/t silver equivalent for 22.4 million ounces.

The latest results build on a string of previous high-grade silver hits at Gavilanes, including 33.9m at 220g/t silver in one hole and 13.2m at 311g/t silver in another. Advance then returned to the same drill pad and sent its latest headline hole beneath the latter intercept, where it struck the bonanza 4120g/t silver hit. With drilling ongoing, metallurgical testwork underway and assays pending for a current diamond hole testing further westerly extensions, plenty of interesting newsflow looks to be on the cards. The company says all results from the current drilling and metallurgical work go towards modelling for a maiden JORC-compliant mineral resource estimate, slated for the final quarter of this year. With a string of high-grade hits now under its belt and a clear path towards a resource, Advance appears to be rounding the corner with considerable pace in Mexico. SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby New Zealand to consider walking away from Super Rugby at major summit Iain Payten September 22, 2026 — 1:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New Zealand will consider walking away from Super Rugby Pacific and Australia, and replacing the 30-year-old competition with a new 8-10 team domestic league. The “bombshell proposal”, which was revealed by the Wellington-based Post newspaper on Tuesday, is one of three options contained in a secret document provided to stakeholders ahead of a major New Zealand Rugby summit on Thursday. Loading The summit, which will see 80 executives from NZR, Super Rugby clubs, provincial unions and the NZ Players Association gather in Wellington, comes as NZR grapples with ways to avoid a looming financial crisis. It was revealed last week in another secret pre-summit document that the NZR are facing losses of $53 million between 2027-2031, even after the massive windfall of a Lions tour in 2029.

Advertisement

With a “structural deficit” of about $16m a year, NZR is searching for ways to cut costs, and one key area of discussion at the summit will be the future of men’s elite competitions. New Zealand runs five Super Rugby teams and 14 National Provincial Championship teams. The NZR document proposes three options for discussion: replacing Super Rugby and the NPC with a domestic professional competition; expanding Super Rugby by two more teams; or continuing Super Rugby and the NPC but with Super and NPC entities combined in Auckland, Waikato, Wellington, Canterbury and Otago. The Crusaders could become part of a domestic New Zealand competition, under a proposal to be dicusssed at a New Zealand summit. Getty Images The option to walk away from Australia and Fiji and go it alone is the most explosive item on the agenda, and informed sources with knowledge of the matter said it was put into the document by the 26 provincial unions, who all get a vote as NZR members and are hugely powerful. The Post reported that the proposal spells out the eight to 10 teams in a national competition would receive up to $8m for player payments and be run by provincial unions. It would open the door for private investment as well, the report said.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Rugby Australia Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity Rugby Australia declined to comment on the Post’s report and a potential exit from Super Rugby by the Kiwi sides. But informed sources with knowledge of both unions said the NZR leadership has made it clear to RA as recently as this week that they remain committed to the trans-Tasman relationship, and to playing in Super Rugby Pacific. The NZR and RA are one year into a five-year broadcast deal for Super Rugby Pacific, and recent discussions between the two unions have covered the possibility of a 10-team competition expanding into Japan and the US. But the expansion to be discussed as an option at the NZR summit is adding two extra teams in New Zealand, presumably from two of the stronger provinces. The document says this option would require “Rugby Australia agreement”, according to the Post. The option to combine the five New Zealand Super Rugby clubs with the provincial unions based in their city would help generate significant savings by eliminating some duplication. The NZR summit, which is an annual event, will consider all proposals before a final position is put to the NZR board in December.

NationalVictoriaRoad safety Russel’s life changed when he hit a pothole. Now, he’s part of a growing wave of litigation Alexander Darling September 22, 2026 — 12:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boxing Day 2022 was turning into a great day for Russel Heggen. As he cruised along Arthurs Seat Road on his Harley-Davidson, the bay spread out before him as he snaked his way back towards his Dromana home. The then 62-year-old didn’t even see the pothole before he hit it. The patch of road had recently been repaired, but Heggen claims the tar had become misshapen with cars driving over it, making a mound at one end and effectively turning it into a ramp. Russel Heggen has filed a personal injury lawsuit against the Department of Transport. He claims the road surface forced him to come off his motorbike on Arthurs Seat Road in 2022. Jason South The impact caused Heggen to involuntarily tighten his grip on the throttle, and he and his Harley went off the road, flying between two trees and off a cliff. Emergency services estimate he travelled 15 metres, but his memory of the crash is fuzzy.

Advertisement

“I was just very lucky to survive,” he said. Luck aside, Heggen was seriously injured, suffering a broken femur and tibia, a fractured pelvis and spine, a collapsed lung and a brain injury. The patched pothole on Arthurs Seat Road that Heggen said acted as a ramp for his motorbike. The ordeal is now detailed in a writ before the Supreme Court, with the 66-year-old joining a growing number of Victorians making public liability claims against road authorities for the serious injuries sustained after accidents allegedly caused by poor road surfaces. In the vast majority of cases, the Transport Accident Commission covers medical expenses related to road accidents. However, under Victorian law, in rare circumstances, road authorities – state and local governments – can be held liable for injuries.

Advertisement

The condition of Victoria’s roads, particularly in regional and rural areas, has become a hot-button issue in the lead-up to the November 28 state election. Concerns boiled over earlier this month when Ballarat motorcyclist Peter “Tiki” Mason, 71, died on the Western Highway after his bike hit a pothole. Several personal injury law firms spoken to by The Age said they had had an increase in inquiries from people wanting compensation for pothole-related road accidents. Peter Mason died on September 14 after his motorcycle hit a pothole on the Western Highway near Ballarat. Facebook, Joe Armao “It’s a wave that’s coming,” Henry Carus, head of Henry Carus & Associates, said. “I think people will get injured while taking evasive action just because of the size of the holes,” he said, noting his firm is overseeing a claim against South Gippsland Shire Council involving a motorcyclist who lost control after hitting a pothole.

Advertisement

Law firm Arnold Thomas & Becker has begun action against Northern Grampians Shire Council on behalf of a woman who suffered several fractures and a torn artery when she lost control of her car near Stawell. Related Series

Victorian election Victoria’s pothole crisis In each case, the lawsuits accuse the respective councils of a litany of failings, including “failing to adequately inspect, maintain, repair or warn road users” about the dangers of the roads in question – the same wording as Heggen’s claim against the Department of Transport. Any recompense the plaintiffs receive as a result of these lawsuits will be in addition to TAC compensation, which all victims of road crashes are entitled to regardless of who is at fault. The existence of a pothole or poor road surface is not enough on its own to prove liability for road authorities. Plaintiffs must be able to prove authorities knew of the threat a section of road posed at the time it caused an accident, and failed to address it appropriately.

Advertisement

In Heggen’s case, his wife, Amanda, and son Mitch took photos of the offending pothole on the same day as the accident. These images are included in the writ for his court action and show a clear mound of road surfacing material sitting several centimetres higher at one edge of the repaired area. Amanda said this turned out to be crucial when her husband eventually decided in 2025 to pursue legal action after receiving less compensation from the TAC than other road crash victims. Heggen about to be flown to The Alfred hospital on the day of the accident. Amanda Heggen “Our lawyers said, ‘That’s all you’re entitled to under the guidelines because no one is at fault’,” she said. “The lawyers said only a few negligence claims had been successful, and they had all had photos and videos, which I gave to them.”

Advertisement

But even a claim with evidence has no certainty of success. Last week, the Supreme Court ruled against a motorcyclist who had been injured the day before Heggen in 2022, on a stretch of road in Reedy Creek, 100 kilometres north of Melbourne. Joshua Masters claimed he lost control of his motorbike after swerving to avoid a pothole and poorly repaired road. But Justice Andrew Keogh concluded Masters had not proved the road authority, in this case Mitchell Shire Council, was liable for the accident. Keogh ruled that while the council had been aware of the defect and inspected it in a careless manner, the road was below the threshold for intervention.

Advertisement

Heggen says he has lost his easy-going nature since the accident and becomes anxious more easily, though he is trying his best to stay positive. Though the writ for Heggen’s case was issued in June, he has been advised it won’t be heard before August 2027. In the meantime, the lifelong member of the Dromana Football Club continues physiotherapy and pool rehabilitation. His wife has also helped by reorganising the layout of their home to assist him, and devising strategies to accommodate his short-term memory issues. “I’m lucky Russel’s resilient. He works with me and never complains about pain,” she said.

Advertisement

Amanda says that pursuing legal action is in part about seeking compensation for Russel’s recovery, but is also about vindication. “At the start of this, Russ said to me all he wanted was someone to acknowledge it was the road surface that caused the incident,” she said. “It’s an issue of public safety. We’re really hopeful that this court case leads to more funding available to fix the root cause of the problem, rather than the government compensating people afterwards.” A Department of Transport spokesperson declined to comment on Heggen’s case as it is before the courts. “Speed, driver fatigue, distractions and a vehicle’s safety features remain the biggest contributors to serious injury crashes,” they said, noting more than 66,000 potholes had been repaired in recent months, with works set to increase to meet Premier Ben Carroll’s pledge of rectifying half a million of them.

title: Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making

SportAFLBrownlow Medal Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making Marc McGowan Updated September 22, 2026 — 12:06pm ,first published September 21, 2026 — 10:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nike was right – it was inevitable. After consecutive runner-up finishes, and a third placing before that, Collingwood champion Nick Daicos is finally a Brownlow medallist. Nick Daicos (right) with his parents Peter and Colleen. AFL Photos Daicos’ major sponsor Nike boldly took out front-page newspaper ads on Monday featuring a photo of the star Magpie, the famous swoosh logo, and the word “Inevitable”. The iconic brand’s confidence was vindicated when the 23-year-old midfielder, wearing custom swoosh cufflinks, won in record-breaking style, beating dual winner Patrick Cripps’ extraordinary 2024 tally of 45 votes with a new count-high total (in the 3-2-1 system) of 47.

Advertisement

The shortest-priced favourite in the event’s history also set a new benchmark of 13 best-on-ground performances and polled in 18 of his 22 matches. Daicos’ victory was sealed with three rounds to go – when he was 10 votes clear – and he eventually equalled Richmond legend Dustin Martin’s record winning margin of 11 votes from 2017, ending his multi-year run of being a beaten Brownlow favourite. “I’ve learnt not to trust the betting markets,” Daicos said after receiving his Brownlow Medal from last year’s winner and former Carey Grammar teammate Matt Rowell. “But, no, there is [relief]. It’s a massive award, and I’m so privileged to be up here. I can’t believe I’m a Brownlow medallist.”

Advertisement

Geelong superstar Bailey Smith (36 votes), Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (34), Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), North Melbourne’s Harry Sheezel, Blue Patrick Cripps and Brisbane’s dual North Smith medallist Will Ashcroft (27) finished behind Daicos. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney was a further vote back on 26 with Zak Butters, but was unable to attend the event after his role in the Pullman Hotel saga. Speaking during the count, Bontempelli said Daicos was the AFL’s best player and had changed the sport with his ability to impact the game with pure hard work and his offensive skills. View post on X

Advertisement

Daicos revealed post-count that his brother and teammate Josh and father Peter – one of Collingwood’s all-time greats – were instrumental in him developing his famed work ethic. Nick and Josh spent countless afternoons as teenagers with their dad at Greythorn Falcons honing their skills. “I feel like from a young age, I probably had more talent [than others] and didn’t work as hard, and had some chats with Dad and Josh as I grew up,” he said. “It was a realisation I wanted to play AFL, and that I needed to train harder. I walk into the club every day, and I’m immensely grateful to be an AFL footballer.

Advertisement

“I think I owe it to the Collingwood Football Club to train with an intensity, and I feel like as a leader at the club, I can’t ask the bloke next to me to put his backside on the line and train really hard if I’m not doing it myself. I try and lead by example.” Daicos’ custom Nike cufflinks. AFL Photos Daicos’ profile and ability to influence young, adoring fans isn’t lost on him, either. He used part of his acceptance speech to single out eight-year-old fan named Logan, who is battling cancer. “I worked closely with him this year, and I think that just shows the platform we can have in impacting people like that – we send videos back and forth throughout the week, and we’re only able to do that and put a smile on his face because we’re playing footy, but then at the same time I think he’s probably taught me more than I’ve taught him,” Daicos explained.

Advertisement

Growing up, footballs were banished from the house by Nick and Josh’s mother, Colleen, but the boys quickly found an alternative. “Dad was creative. He’d scrunch the toilet paper up into this little oval shape, and then we’d go to Officeworks, get some sticky tape, and wrap it the whole way around,” he said. “I think it worked for everyone because we weren’t getting the red marks on the wall, so Mum was happy, too.” Daicos’ Brownlow victory followed him also collecting the AFL Players’ Association’s MVP and AFL Coaches’ Association’s player of the year, becoming the first footballer to claim all three since Lachie Neale six years ago.

Advertisement

His latest honour makes him arguably the most accomplished young player ever, swelling a resume that already includes the Magpies’ 2023 premiership and four All-Australian selections. Daicos will almost certainly win a third Copeland Trophy next month as well. He is the 10th Magpie to win a Brownlow Medal and first since Dane Swan 15 years ago, also joining Syd Coventry, brothers Albert and Harry Collier, Marcus Whelan, Des Fothergill, Len Thompson, Peter Moore and Nathan Buckley. Daicos polled maximum votes in each of his first three games – either side of the Magpies’ round two bye – before he was a late withdrawal with a corked calf against Brisbane. That was the only match he missed all season.

Advertisement

Daicos proudly shows off the 2026 Brownlow Medal after a record-breaking night. AFL Photos Daicos’ streak of maximum votes ended in a round five loss to Fremantle, where he still polled one off a 31-disposal effort, and it was enough to break an early deadlock with fellow great Bontempelli. Zak Butters briefly snatched a one-vote lead in round 10, but Daicos was back on top a round later when he was best afield against West Coast as Scott Pendlebury broke the VFL/AFL games record with his 433rd appearance. Smith drew level with the gun Pie on 23 votes in round 14, with Butters a single vote back, before Daicos shot away again a round later with three votes after a 41-touch masterclass at Port Adelaide’s expense.

Advertisement

That was when Daicos made his move, turning an entertaining count with superstars spread across the leaderboard into a demolition, like a Melbourne Cup winner turning for home. The man in the No.35 secured maximum votes in six straight matches between rounds 15 and 20 in an incredible purple patch to kick clear of the field and end any doubt about the result. Daicos polled 11 votes to finish equal 27th in his debut season in 2022; came third with 28 votes in 2023; second with 38 votes in 2024; and second with 32 votes last year. Umpires had access to player statistics for the first time this year to help with voting.
