Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears QLD demerger frees Broken Hill for SA gold focus Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 22, 2026 — 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Broken Hill Gold has completed the strategic demerger of its North Queensland portfolio, transferring its Alice River gold and St George gold-antimony projects to Manda Resources. The deal clears the decks for an all-out focus on its White Dam gold operation in South Australia. The transaction hands Manda Broken Hill’s 100 per cent interest in Alice River and its St George earn-in rights for 64M Manda shares valued at $16M, plus $650,000 cash payable on Manda’s ASX admission. Subject to shareholder approval, all the shares, valued at 25 cents each, will be distributed in specie to eligible shareholders, retaining their exposure to the Queensland story. Under indicative terms announced in June, they would receive one Manda share for every 6.76 Broken Hill shares, with the final ratio set at the record date. Broken Hill Gold’s operational gold processing plant at White Dam in South Australia, now the company’s sole focus following its Queensland demerger. ASX-listed mining junior Emerald Resources has also brought heavyweight backing and a safe pair of hands to Manda. The company initially invested $6.4M into Manda’s $9M pre-IPO seed raising for a 49 per cent shareholding. It has since flagged another $4.25M investment in the initial public offering, which is expected to raise at least $21M, subject to market conditions. Emerald intends to maintain a 19.9 per cent Manda holding at listing. Manda has also wrapped up its acquisition of Territory Minerals, bringing the Tregoora, Northcote, Atric and Reedy gold projects under the same roof. Alice River contributes 26.8 million tonnes at 1.00 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 854,000 ounces, while Territory adds 480,000 ounces, giving the portfolio 1.33 million ounces across more than 1700 square kilometres.

Advertisement

‘The demerger means we are now exceptionally well-positioned to execute on our focused strategy, with maiden production at White Dam achieved and cashflow from gold production imminent.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes Manda has also strengthened its leadership, putting veteran exploration geologist Tara French at the helm as chief executive officer. French brings more than 25 years’ experience and was most recently Cazaly Resources’ managing director after serving as Regis Resources’ general manager, exploration. At Alice River, Manda inherits plenty to chase along a 30km prospective strike on the Alice River Fault Zone, part of a regional-scale intrusion-related system Broken Hill has compared geologically with globally significant gold systems Fort Knox in the United States and Hemi in Western Australia. Its nearby St George project adds a 905-square-kilometre gold-antimony footprint, where exploration has defined more than 20km of mineralised and geochemical strike, yet drilling has tested just 200m. That leaves plenty of room to build on early high-grade antimony and gold hits. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “This strategic demerger is a highly compelling transaction. Having Emerald Resources’ management driving this new vehicle is a real endorsement of the geological potential at the Alice River and St George Projects. Manda’s concurrent acquisition of Territory Minerals will create a dominant explorer in a region with clear multimillion-ounce potential.”

Advertisement

Attention now turns to Manda’s listing. Its prospectus and Broken Hill’s notice of meeting are targeted for early November, with the shareholder vote due in early December and Manda’s targeted ASX admission in mid-December. Distributed shares are expected to face 12 months of mandatory escrow from their issue date. Back in South Australia, White Dam is now primed to take centre stage for Broken Hill. The project has more than 50 prospects, many lightly tested at depth, with more than 30,000m of reverse-circulation and diamond drilling planned over the next 18 months to probe its deeper gold-copper potential. The operation produced roughly 180,000 ounces between 2010 and 2018 and comes with open pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant, giving the company a brownfields springboard rather than a standing-start development. The near-minegrounds span Vertigo and Hannaford alongside the emerging Icebreaker gold-copper discovery, with existing processing infrastructure providing a ready pathway for shallow oxide material. Its latest Vertigo update lifted White Dam’s global resource to 5.2 million tonnes at 0.7g/t gold for 118,496 ounces, including 24,300 indicated ounces at Vertigo. Mining studies will assess an oxide heap-leach restart, once the current material on the leach pad has been processed, with a prefeasibility study planned after the remaining shallow resources are drilled and updated.

Advertisement

Now, with two rigs in the field, Broken Hill can push ahead on shallow oxide drilling while accelerating the deeper sulphide hunt at Vertigo and Icebreaker. With the Queensland baton passed to Manda, Broken Hill’s gold pendulum has swung firmly south. At White Dam, the clock is already running on both a return to open-pit mining and the hunt for a deeper gold-copper prize. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? title: ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsOil Opinion ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 22, 2026 — 12:04pm

September 22, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump White House is under mounting pressure to “do something” about the price of diesel in the US. That something would have dire consequences for much of the world, including the US – and Australia, the world’s biggest per-capita user of the fuel. A lengthening queue of Republicans, including Senate majority leader John Thune, have called for the US to consider banning or restricting exports of diesel after its average domestic price hit another record of $US6.51 ($9.14) a gallon on Monday. That’s about 75 per cent higher than the average US price a year ago. The price of diesel has smashed records, just weeks before the midterm elections. AP With farmers, who are about to start their autumn harvest season, the heartland constituency for Republicans, it isn’t surprising that their political representatives, mainly Republicans, are becoming anxious in the lead-up to November’s midterm elections. Where the White House initially waved off suggestions of limiting diesel exports, arguing – rightly – that it could be counter-productive, there have been signs recently that the attitude is thawing as the elections loom.

Advertisement

Donald Trump appears to be very aware of the political implications, but is misdiagnosing the cause of the big spike in prices. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House Behind Trump’s bluster there’s a sobering realisation he is losing the public At the weekend, he repeated his call for Ukraine to stop its drone attacks on Russian refineries, almost all of which – with the exception of a handful of hard-to-reach plants in Siberia – have been damaged by Ukrainian bombing. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended.”

Advertisement

As a result of the Ukrainian attacks, Russia – a major exporter of diesel before its invasion of the country – has halted all exports and is now importing diesel, mainly from India. Related Article Exclusive

Blood Oil Funding Putin: ‘Blood oil’ imports from major Asian supplier surge While that is contributing to the surge in diesel prices globally, it isn’t the primary cause. Last year, Russia exported about 800,000 barrels a day of diesel and gas oil, making it the world’s second-largest exporter behind the US. The Middle East, as a region, however, exported about 1.5 million barrels a day. With those Middle Eastern exports now reduced by more than 50 per cent, it is Trump’s war on Iran that’s the major influence on the diesel shortages that are driving up prices.

Advertisement

It is Trump’s war on Iran that’s the major influence on the diesel shortages that are driving up prices. It hasn’t helped that China, a major processor of crude oil into distillates including diesel, halted exports earlier this year after the attacks on Iran. It subsequently resumed them but, with its inventories at their lowest level for more than a year, is expected to reintroduce export curbs. Moreover, unlike crude supply, where the end of hostilities in the Middle East would see a rapid rebound in supply, elevated diesel prices are likely to be a feature of the global markets for months after the war’s conclusion, if not years, because of the extensive damage to the region’s refineries. The same timelines would apply to Russia’s infrastructure if that war were to end. The Senate’s majority leader John Thune (left) is among the Republicans urging Trump to limit diesel exports. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin What US Republicans are urging the White House to do to “stop the bleeding” ranges from a complete ban on diesel exports to restrictions that link permitted exports to domestic diesel prices. There are also calls for the scrapping of fuel excises and financial subsidies for farmers and truckers.

Advertisement

An export ban would keep the diesel that the US currently exports within the US, but would have devastating consequences for those countries that have become increasingly reliant on America’s record exports since the war in the Middle East erupted. In Europe, where record prices are the equivalent of a $US190 a barrel oil price and inventories are at record lows for this time of the year, there are already supply shortages even before the region heads into the northern winter. Diesel-dependent Asia is just as vulnerable, if not more so. Related Article Exclusive

Energy Supply crunch hits Australian fuel distributors at east-coast ports But any restrictions in exports could have adverse consequences for the US itself, too. While it is the world’s largest diesel exporter, it does import about 165,000 barrels a day. That’s because much of its refining capacity is on the US Gulf Coast, with limited pipeline infrastructure to the north-east and west coasts. In any event, most of the pipelines linking refineries to their end markets are operating at or near capacity.

Advertisement

An export ban would see prices surge further in those regions which the infrastructure doesn’t reach, and lead to a build-up of inventories within the refineries. The US accounts for about 1.5 million barrels a day of the daily 8 million barrels or so of the global seaborne trade in diesel. A US export ban would see global prices soar further, with flow-on consequences for those US regions dependent on imported product. More broadly, with an export ban or restrictions, there’d be more diesel held within the US. But the refineries, which have been operating at close to full capacity, would reduce their crude oil purchases because they’d be physically incapable of delivering much more than they do today, let alone the 30 per cent or so increase in diesel supply required to absorb the diverted export volumes. Even a brief relief from high prices might save a few seats and help protect Trump from the inevitability of a lame-duck second half to his presidency Areas close to the refineries might get lower prices, but the rest of the country would probably experience even higher prices.

Advertisement

There’s also the problem that, unless crude oil prices fell sharply, refinery margins would be squeezed if diesel prices fell, likely leading to reduced, rather than increased, production. Refinery profits and export revenues would be lost and the refiners’ relationships with their offshore customers would be damaged, without any lasting benefit in the form of lower domestic prices. Related Article Analysis

US politics At half-full stadium, Trump makes desperate pitch to save the midterms So, if both a total or partial ban on diesel exports are likely to be counter-productive, why would senior Republicans be forcing it onto the White House agenda? It’s the elections, of course, where control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, is likely to be determined by cost-of-living issues, with gasoline and diesel prices front-of-mind with voters.

Advertisement

Diesel, because of the role it plays in transport, shipping and agriculture, is also a meaningful influence on the inflation rate. The longer prices remain at record levels, the more those prices are likely to feed into the elevated prices of food and consumer goods generally, forcing the inflation rate to remain high and increasing the likelihood of further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, perhaps as early as next month – just weeks ahead of the midterms. It is apparent that there are some in the White House who are aware that, while a ban might cause an initial drop in the price of diesel, the reprieve would be temporary and the longer-term consequences would probably be damaging to the economy, businesses and consumers. Loading Yet given the proximity of the elections, even a brief relief from high prices might save a few seats and help protect Trump from the inevitability of a lame-duck second half to his presidency, and the investigations and impeachments that would flow from a Democrat majority in the House.

Advertisement

title: ‘Nonsense’: Major racing club blames jockeys for track drama, dismisses safety concerns
text:
Advertisement

SportRacingVictorian racing ‘Nonsense’: Major racing club blames jockeys for track drama, dismisses safety concerns Danny Russell September 22, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Melbourne Racing Club has dismissed any concerns about track safety at Caulfield Racecourse, despite images of jockeys lifting large clumps of turf in the home straight before Saturday’s group 1 race meeting. The club released a strongly worded statement on Tuesday claiming the jockeys’ pre-race safety concerns were “nonsense”, and said a decision to move the running rail and delay the start of the meeting was unnecessary. A clod of dirt lifted from the Caulfield track before race one. Getty Images The MRC’s declaration that there was never any issue with the Caulfield surface comes in a week that they boasted of a record $281.4 million turnover in the past financial year despite suffering a $10.6 million loss. Saturday’s delay at Caulfield came after a group of jockeys identified loose “plugs” in sections of the track before the first event, leading stewards to order maintenance staff to make last-minute alterations.

Advertisement

Plugs are large, turf covered clumps of dirt that are wedged into divots to make them safe for horses to run over. MRC CEO Tanya Fullarton said an internal review “found no safety issue” with Saturday’s track. Caulfield track staff moved the running rail before Saturday’s meeting started. Getty Images “The turf plugs were correctly installed, the track as presented was safe for racing and the rail did not need to be moved,” Fullarton said. “The track subsequently raced safely and fairly throughout the meeting. Dozens of exactly the same turf plugs remained on other sections of the track that continued to be raced on after the rail movement, with no issues for jockeys and horses.

Advertisement

“The jockeys clearly did not understand how turf plugs work. The jockeys’ claim that being able to pull the tops off the plugs somehow showed that the track was unsafe is nonsense. “Turf plugs are routinely installed a few days before a race day and are always able to be physically pulled up, as grass plugs take at least two weeks to bind with the rest of the turf profile. “This has been standard practice for over 25 years and is not a problem – they remain in place while horses gallop over them, with no risk to jockeys or horses.” To avoid future issues, Racing Victoria has enlisted former champion jockey Damien Oliver to conduct independent track inspections for the next 12 weeks. Oliver will inspect the surface for this Sunday’s group 1 Manikato Stakes meeting at Caulfield, and will continue to do so throughout the spring, including all Flemington meetings.

Advertisement

Related Article Victorian racing Legal feuds, boardroom battles and a 24-year-old taking on racing’s elite He will report to Racing Victoria stewards before each race day starts to provide a safety assessment of the tracks. “Saturday showed the importance of ensuring any concerns about a racing surface are properly assessed, with the appropriate technical input, before significant decisions are made on race day,” Fullarton said. “The stewards were placed in an extremely difficult position, with concerns raised by jockeys less than an hour before the first race. “With the limited time available, they were unable to properly consult with our track team about the purpose, installation and condition of the plugs before making the incorrect decision to move the rail.

Advertisement

“Our track team complied with that direction so the meeting could proceed, but this is not how these issues should have to be dealt with on race day.” Despite the club dismissing any safety concerns, the rail will be moved out 13m for Sunday’s Manikato meeting, which has been transferred from Moonee Valley. “The reason the rail isn’t moving to the true position is to protect the track for the Caulfield Cup carnival,” a club spokesperson said. It is not the first time the MRC has come under fire from punters this year, following criticism for the standard of its tracks at Caulfield and Sandown during the winter months. On top of that, two barrier attendants were lucky to escape injury in June when starting barriers were accidentally reversed into a lake in the middle of Sandown Racecourse. They were later fished out with a crane.

Advertisement

“It would probably be a good idea for MRC to change their name back to VATC … Very Amateur Turf Club as the legend of racing writers used to refer to it,” prominent owner Nick Williams posted on X on Saturday. Jockey Patrick Moloney told Racing.com the track surface was fine after the pre-race alterations, but the changes had made it “really awkward” to navigate for riders. The MRC released its annual general report on Monday, revealing a second consecutive substantial loss, this year’s $10.6 million deficit following $14.7 million in the 2025 financial year. The club forked out $10.9 million in bank interest in the past year on $197.7 million in borrowings, which it said it expected to clear with the sale of land at Caulfield to Mount Scopus College for $195 million. The Jewish school signed an agreement to purchase the land in December 2024 and was given two years to exercise that option. The deal has still not been finalised.

Advertisement

The MRC now has 17 poker machine venues after recently buying two new outlets - The Cumberland and the Cheltenham Club - and these venues brought in $128.2 million last year and made a $48.3 million profit. Related Article Victorian racing Caulfield order track safety review, as big guns firm for Cox Plate and Caulfield Cup “We continued to grow addition revenue streams to support the club and reinvest in racing,” Fullarton said. MRC chairman Cameron Fisher said reducing debt remained the club board’s key priority, while the committee was committed to racing at Sandown. The club will hold its annual general meeting on Thursday night and will announce the results of its recent board elections during which 24-year-old newcomer Fergus Ewart stood against sitting members Caitrin Kelly, Belinda Meyers and Robyn Gray. Jason Derulo | The Last Dance Tour ★★★

Rod Laver Arena, September 21 When Jason Derulo named his tour “The Last Dance”, he meant it. From the moment the Floridian singer appears on stage, his body does not stop moving. Jason Derulo performs at Rod Laver Arena in Melbourne on September 21, 2026. Richard Clifford Surrounded by perhaps the bendiest backup dancers in history, he gyrates, moonwalks, and pops and locks until sweat pours off his brow, wiped away occasionally by a very lucky hand towel. For the Millennials in the crowd, of which there are many, the first hour is like being transported back to a 2010s house party – appropriate, given it’s Derulo’s 37th birthday.

Advertisement

Older hits like Whatcha Say and Wiggle have 40-year-olds screaming like teens. Backing tracks do much of the heavy lifting, allowing Derulo to slip and slide across the stage. But when he does sing – through a sassy little Britney mic – it’s smooth as butter, hitting falsetto notes like it’s nothing. Newer songs like Acapulco and Savage Love, meanwhile, lean into his meme status, getting the crowd to shout the TikTok slang term “sheesh” as loud as they can. Jason Derulo is undeniably a gifted and polished performer. Richard Clifford Hearing him sing his own name – the famously corny audio tag – in perfect pitch is both hilarious and magnificent. His energy is best described as cheesy, especially when whipping out the viral Mi Chico TikTok dance. But through sheer enthusiasm, Derulo gets away with it. Like with most house parties, however, Derulo doesn’t quite know when to pack things up. He throws everything but the kitchen sink onto the stage – pyro, confetti, streamers, a DJ hype man, more animal print than most zoos.

Advertisement

We travel from “Derulo’s lab” to his jungle, velvet room and volcano, all of which are signposted by strangely irrelevant AI videos of cherry blossom robots, vampires crying blood and futuristic merpeople. By the time he gets to Don’t Wanna Go Home, the AI videos and bass-heavy dance breaks blur together, making it difficult to distinguish each song. This is especially a shame when showcasing Let Me Be, a new track that he has only performed live twice before. Jason Derulo threw everything but the kitchen sink onto the stage. Richard Clifford Though the energy noticeably lifts again when Talk Dirty and Want to Want Me strike up – cashing in on the Derulo nostalgia – we’re already as exhausted as the back-up dancer who just did 10 backflips back-to-back. Derulo is undeniably a gifted and polished performer. Every move is precise, down to the way he flips his microphone and coyly lifts his shirt. But at this last dance, there’s simply too much to feast our eyes upon.

title: As world leaders arrive in the US, there's one question they want answered
text:
In brief World leaders have signed a statement on AI regulation ahead of a leaders' meeting at the UN General Assembly this week.

Anthony Albanese has been praised as a "trailblazer" for Australia's under-16 social media ban.

In the hyper-colour, futuristic crush of New York City's Times Square, a man who calls himself "Scientific" reflects on the march of artificial intelligence (AI).

He told SBS News the realities of AI have already arrived, with power both awesome and deeply confronting.

"You got to adapt with it. If you don’t adapt, in 10 years we are going to become extinct," he said.

Scientific is a musician. He wants more regulation of the technology companies.

"It's going left and right with this artificial intelligence … right now it’s acting like it's human.

"If it has too much freedom over creativity, and gets the credit, what do they need us for?"

He's not alone. Everyone we spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted tourist magnet expressed concern about where the technology is leading humanity.

Another man urged some regulation be fast-tracked to ensure that AI agents don't decide humans are doing dangerous things and "get rid of them".

That's despite most people we spoke to also conceding they rely on ChatGPT and other AI assistants to help streamline their work and home lives.

Scientific, a musician, wants greater regulation over big tech companies pushing AI. Source: SBS News / Anna Henderson

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has played a "central role" in crafting a statement alongside a broad coalition of international leaders, calling for control of frontier artificial intelligence models.

That statement was publicly released on Tuesday ahead of the United Nations General Assembly leaders' week.

Signatories represent Norway, Finland, Bahrain, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Germany, Iceland, Ireland, Kazakhstan, Kenya, Latvia, Moldova, the Netherlands, Singapore, Spain, South Africa, Türkiye and the United Arab Emirates

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has also signed up, and in a meeting with Albanese referred to him as a "trailblazer" in reference to Australia's social media laws.

READ MORE We came to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos

The leaders of other nations are being encouraged to add heft to the message, which acknowledges AI's power to improve people's lives but sounds the alarm about safety risks if the technology is mismanaged.

"Leading scientists and executives are warning that the pace of development could outpace our ability to manage emerging risks," the statement said.

"To realise AI's potential, industry, governments and society must act now. We must address these risks and strengthen oversight — without widening the gap between countries in access to the benefits of AI."

"AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law."

It commends companies that have transparent safety controls and endorses common standards that encourage the sharing of safety incidents.

The statement proposes an international institution to set standards and provide oversight to "convene states when capability thresholds are crossed".

Albanese wants to build on the international reputation he's achieved through the under-16s social media ban by helping shape how the world approaches the AI challenge.

"If it's going to be successful, then we need to make sure that humans are at the centre of everything that occurs," Albanese said.

In some ways, the world leaders who address the UN this week are a sideshow. The real draw is the main AI negotiations set to take place between the United States and Chinese presidents at the White House later this week.

But this statement is intended to lobby US President Donald Trump to consider further protections. So far, he's indicated that’s not his preference.

"We hope for a positive meeting," Albanese said.

"Other nations are putting forward their national interest.

"Australians do want to know that artificial intelligence won't be in control of us."

Whether the tech industry would comply with the demands of UN member states is unclear.

Sam Altman, CEO of ChatGPT developer OpenAI, is expected to address an open session of the UN Security Council this week.

Many people SBS News spoke to in Manhattan's billboard-encrusted Times Square expressed concern about where AI is leading humanity. Source: SBS News / Anna Henderson

Back in Times Square, a man in a gorilla costume poses for photos, while smart glasses flash up on one of the hundreds of advertising screens behind him.

The companies advancing AI know they are the giant gorillas in this AI race.

title: Trump faces media revolt after banning three outlets from White House
text:
In brief Major US networks halted White House pool coverage after Trump banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico.

The outlets are suing, arguing the ban violated press freedom and constitutional protections.

US television networks staged an extraordinary revolt Monday when they effectively boycotted coverage of President Donald Trump in protest at his decision to ban three leading outlets from the White House.

CNN, MS NOW and Politico also went to court after Trump on Saturday ordered them to be barred, as the 80-year-old Republican stepped up his years-long assault on the US media.

As a result of the row, Trump's opening of his cherished new White House helipad and his trip to the United Nations General Assembly were proceeding without live television coverage.

In a rare move, US broadcasters ABC, CBS, NBC, Fox News, and CNN said on Tuesday that they were halting "pool" coverage of the White House — where a broadcaster films on behalf of all television outlets for the day — in solidarity with CNN.

CNN had been scheduled to serve on Tuesday as the White House TV pool.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should restrict a news organization because it objects to its reporting," ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC said in a statement.

The result is an almost unprecedented test of wills between the Trump administration and the press, in a critical week during which Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting the White House.

Media 'like cancer'

There will be no live TV of Trump's meetings with foreign leaders at the UN in New York, an annual forum that is closely watched around the world.

Meanwhile, the ribbon-cutting ceremony for the giant granite helipad on the South Lawn was only streamed on the White House's website — and Trump's comments were completely inaudible.

Several photo news organisations working at the White House decided to delay the release of photographs of Trump at the helipad in solidarity with the three banned media organisations.

Trump was unrepentant, branding the media a "cancer" and a threat to national security.

"The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish," Trump said on his Truth Social network.

"It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America."

Vice President JD Vance — a former CNN commentator before his move into politics — accused the outlets of disseminating "left-wing propaganda."

"They can still report. They still have the access to free speech. They're just not going to get an office in the White House anymore," he told reporters.

Trump's ban, however, went further than simply revoking office space from the outlets.

Journalists from CNN, MS NOW and Politico were denied any access to the White House grounds on Saturday and had their passes confiscated.

In their lawsuit, the three organisations asked for a temporary restraining order against the ban on the grounds that it violates the First Amendment of the US Constitution, which upholds the right to a free press.

"This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles," the organisations said in a court filing.

A US district judge set a hearing on the complaint for Wednesday.

Press passes confiscated

Trump's sudden announcement of the ban on Saturday stunned the media — and reportedly many in his own administration.

The president has not detailed what prompted the ban, but said in response to a question from a reporter from the Agence France-Presse news agency in the Oval Office on Friday that it was "really just cumulative stories over the last two years."

Trump warned on Saturday that other outlets could face a similar fate, without saying which.

The billionaire former reality TV star has long attacked media outlets that have aired critical coverage of his campaigns and administrations, repeatedly blasting the press as the "enemy of the people."

But the ban comes at a time when his approval ratings are at record lows, his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in November's midterm elections, and the Iran war drags on with no end in sight.

title: Would giving Australians $75,000 change the country's future?
text:
in brief Australia faces a choice between higher immigration or having more babies to fix an ageing workforce and shrinking tax base.

Experts say migration is the most effective strategy to staff essential sectors like aged care long term.

Australia will need to boost its population to support the elderly and the economy in the long term, experts warn, after the government's latest Intergenerational Report (IGR) found that people are expected to live longer and have fewer children.

The report landed as politicians float the idea of bringing back the Howard-era baby bonus and argue over the need to reduce migration.

Independent MP Bob Katter has recently suggested an up-front cash payment of $75,000 per child would reverse the declining birth rate, which is now expected to fall to just 1.34 children per woman by 2065.

The argument was dismissed by Treasurer Jim Chalmers and Nationals leader Matt Canavan, who said on Monday that family support policy should be more than just "here's some cash".

However, Australia does face challenging demographic questions, with experts saying the choice will come down to more migrants or more babies.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"We will have a large pool of elderly people that we have to support," Dr Pelin Akyol, research manager at the economic think tank The e61 Institute, told SBS News.

"If we have a smaller pool of people working, then it will be a big fiscal problem in this country — and in every country."

Global and domestic surveys show that most people want to have more children than they end up having, owing to cultural, social, and economic constraints which are difficult to address.

"With AI and everything else going on right now, it is hard to know what will happen," Akyol said. "But what we know at this point is that it's going to affect the economy in a bad way".

The fertility illusion

While the IGR highlights a collapsing birth rate, demographers caution that official metrics paint a distorted picture of Australian family choices.

Peter McDonald, emeritus professor of demography at the Australian National University, told SBS News that the country's reliance on international students and temporary visa holders skewed the headline Total Fertility Rate (TFR).

Temporary migrants are often young adults aged 20 to 35 who are in higher education or the early stages of their career. While they are counted as potential mothers, they "hardly have any births," McDonald said, which drives the TFR down.

Previous Intergenerational Reports have predicted that Australia would have a higher fertility rate.

"That's one of the central reasons why Australia's fertility rate has been falling because the temporary population's been rising," he said.

The birth rate for women born in Australia is around 1.64, higher than the Australian Bureau of Statistics headline fertility rate of 1.48. While this is still below the replacement rate of 2.1, Akyol said the immigration influence on TFR is different in Australia than in other comparable nations.

"In Germany, migrants have higher fertility rate than natives," she said. "But in Australia, it is the opposite".

READ MORE Cheryll tried to get pregnant for years. One thing sealed her decision to stop

McDonald also warns against placing too much faith in the long-term projections of the IGR — which assumes net overseas migration will remain flat at 235,000 annually for the next four decades — and that immigration and total births can't be viewed separately as they are "not independent of each other".

"If you can tell me what the birth rate is going to be in 10 years, you're a better man than me," he said. "But if you can tell me what it is in 40 years, then you're a miracle worker."

Is a baby bonus the answer?

Katter's proposed return to former treasurer Peter Costello's cash payment for each newborn child would cost upwards of an estimated $22.5 billion a year for the present 300,000 babies born each year in Australia.

Akyol's research into the 2004 policy indicates that cash incentives do increase the fertility rate, but the effect is "not huge" and, given how different the world is today, "it is not guaranteed we will see a similar effect".

While a $75,000 payment is "huge" compared to the $3,000 of the original policy and "might have an effect", Akyol doubted this was the best use of money when other factors like support benefits also play a key role in family decisions.

Independent Queensland federal MP Bob Katter has said a $75,000 payment per baby would reverse Australia's declining birth rate — experts disagree. Source: AAP

McDonald said Australia's tax system has become too narrowly focused on early childcare, making raising older children harder for working families.

"Today, about 58 per cent of families get no family allowance for their children," he said. "It's not just about very young children... supporting families with children is also about supporting older children, and we've gone a long, long way away from doing that."

A median worker claiming both employer and state parental leave would already receive around $48,700 before tax, something McDonald said disadvantages those without full-time employment. Instead of re-introducing lump-sum payments, he calls for a broader review of child equity.

"I think there's a need for an inquiry into the system of child support payments, to deal with two issues: one is the inequity of the system for very young children, and two, the lack of support for older children," he said.

"Children are a social good.... so I think there is justification for supporting families with children; it's called horizontal equity."

"Horizontal equity used to be quite a big thing back in the 1980s ... I think it needs to be revisited."

A national trade-off

To offset a declining taxpayer base, the IGR highlights increasing older workforce participation and leveraging artificial intelligence to automate labour gaps.

However, McDonald questioned the feasibility of expecting Australians to work deeper into their 60s and 70s.

"A lot of people, particularly those who work in physically demanding jobs, do not want to work beyond pension age. They've had enough," he said.

"AI is going to make a big difference to future labour force needs, but AI is not going to wipe the bottoms of people in aged care."

Akyol said current debates around migration could soon flip as birth rates drop across the globe, including in key migrant origin countries such as China and India. With a shrinking global talent pool, nations could shift from seeking to restrict migration to actively competing for skilled workers.

"In the long run, there might really be a competition for getting the best migrants," Akyol said. "Because in all developed countries, fertility rate has been decreasing... and it seems like there is no hope that it will just turn back and increase again."

"There is no easy solution here. There is a trade-off with every kind of policy."

Relying on immigration is the most direct mechanism to address workforce shortages in sectors like aged care, which are already under strain, McDonald said — something he said the government has failed to communicate in its messaging.

"The IGR shows the advantage of a higher level of migration for the federal government's bottom line," McDonald said. "Migrants make our prospects of dealing with a future aged population much better."

title: 'Rules need to be upheld': Australia's push to change a contentious UN power
text:
Australia would push to reform the United Nations if given a seat on its Security Council, Foreign Minister Penny Wong said on Monday, as she joined Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York for the United Nations General Assembly.

Speaking with SBS News, Wong said Russia's use of veto powers to exempt itself from repercussions during its invasion of Ukraine was an example of where Australia would seek reform.

"We've had a longstanding position as a country of reform of the veto, and we know it's been misused previously," Wong told SBS World News chief political correspondent Anna Henderson in New York.

"What happened in relation to Russia's invasion of Ukraine was that a permanent member of the Security Council used its veto to prevent any action being taken for its own breach of the charter. That was an example where we would like reform."

Fifteen countries sit on the Security Council, and its five permanent members — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — have the right to veto any resolution or decision.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In 2022, Russia vetoed a Security Council resolution that described its attempts to unlawfully annex four regions of Ukraine as “a threat to international peace and security”, demanding Russia “immediately, completely and unconditionally withdraw all of its military forces” from Ukrainian territory. Ten of fifteen members had voted in favour of the resolution, while four abstained.

Wong said that Australia was "for reform", but that Australians were "very practical people".

"We recognise rules need to be upheld; the UN needs to be reformed.

"We want to make sure, where it really matters, that we continue to be part of setting the direction about that reform."

Wong has backed Albanese's bid for a seat on the council, which Australia has not held since 2014. Asked whether the veto powers in their current state rendered the campaign redundant, Wong stood by the pursuit.

"We might be distant from New York, but we are not distant from the rest of the world, and the world does have an effect on what happens in our economy, in our lives.

"So what I would say is we want to be able to advocate for Australia's interests in every forum that matters, and the UN Security Council matters."

International law under 'pressure'

International law is under a "great deal of pressure", Wong said, but the best response would be for countries to "come together" and advocate for the observance of international law.

"You've got two options, don't you? You can throw your hands up and say, 'I give up'. Or you can say, 'This actually matters to many countries.'

"We're not a superpower, but we're a country with substance and power to work with others to try and ensure that we hold onto the rules that matter."

Asked whether Australia could hold the United States to account over accusations around the war in Iran, as well as its actions in Venezuela, Wong said it was a task for the international community to work out the rules that "we really want to hold on to, that matter to us".

"I think trading arrangements matter to us. They certainly matter to Australia, and we've been very clear about our difference with the Trump administration."

But Australia does not intend to join its like-minded international partners in broader sanctions on Israeli settlements on the West Bank, Wong said, referring to "targeted sanctions" announced earlier this month as the UK banned trade in the occupied territories, and nine European countries said they were considering the same.

"I've announced already that we would engage in targeted sanctions," Wong said, noting that no country that had announced it would engage in the sanctions on a blanket basis had yet implemented them.

"And we certainly will be working with them as they do that to understand how they intend to deal with that," she said, and added that she has a "very clear intention" of engaging in more action against settlements, "which are an obstacle to peace", and "engaging in behaviour which makes two states less likely" in the case of the E-1 settlement, a contentious development plan for a 12-square-kilometre corridor in the West Bank.

"We'll continue to work closely with our like-minded countries just as we did a year ago, when, with others, we recognised the state of Palestine, which was part of the precursor to the peace plan, which we want to see implemented."

title: Does Australia's favourite travel destination hold the secret to a longer life?
text:
In brief Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia.

Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.

This article contains a reference to suicide.

Long famous for the longevity of its citizens, Japan surpassed a record 100,000 people aged 100 or older this year.

According to the country's health, labour and welfare ministry, Japan's number of centenarians increased for the 56th consecutive year to 107,677 — 88 per cent of whom were women.

Ageing populations are increasing worldwide, including in Australia, where life expectancy, already the third-highest in the world behind Monaco and Japan, is expected to climb over the next 40 years.

According to the Australian government's latest Intergenerational Report, released on Monday, Australia's ageing population is expected to transform the economy.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

As we look to a future with an older population and a longer life expectancy, what lessons can Australia take from Japan?

Henry Brodaty, Scientia professor of ageing and mental health at the University of New South Wales, said there were some obvious differences between Japan and Australia, notably the former's healthier lifestyle: Japanese people largely eat fewer high-fat and ultra-processed foods.

"They eat a lot of fish, which has been associated with a better diet and a lower risk of dementia," Brodaty told SBS News.

He said that social isolation and alcohol intake, both risk factors for dementia, were lower in Japan than in Australia, though Japan had high rates of high blood pressure and vascular disease. Stress levels were also much higher than Australia's.

"In fact, our suicide rate is about 12 to 100,000," Brodaty said. "And theirs is about 16 to 100,000."

Urban supports for longevity

Professor Marco Amati from RMIT University's Centre for Urban Research said Japan has elderly care baked into its urban planning.

"One of the biggest challenges for Australia is to do with aged care facilities, which have many issues; notably, there was a royal commission into that," he told SBS News.

Amati said Japan was good at providing end-of-life care for the elderly, with a clear commitment to providing social housing, public transport, and amenities to a high enough standard as to allow people to "age in place". Amati described this as the "Holy Grail", the "most dignified way to age".

"Everybody would prefer to remain at home, surrounded by your community, age in place, and pass away in a familiar environment," he said.

"If you have a situation where people own their own home, and they have to sell their house to go into aged care, that can be very traumatic."

By contrast, in Japan, housing communities are set up to allow ageing in place, including in rental accommodation or in public housing, and for people with early-onset dementia.

READ MORE Aged care giant refunds $200,000 to residents over disputed living fees

In such places, technological advancements have enabled the monitoring of elderly residents in non-obtrusive ways, ensuring that any end-of-life incidents do not go unnoticed — a common issue for elderly people with few surviving relatives.

Amati said that while similar housing approaches may not be achievable in Australia, they were still useful to know about.

"In Australia it's a whole different mix," he said. "But having that kind of a commitment or even knowing that it exists is useful to know."

Australia's biggest threat to long life

The biggest threat to long life in Australia is dementia, which in 2024 overtook cancer and heart disease to become Australia's biggest killer nationally.

Brodaty quoted recent figures from a US study published in the journal Nature: for people aged 55, the lifetime risk of dementia was 42 per cent.

"It's a scary statistic," Brodaty said.

READ MORE Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture

The earlier people embrace brain health, the higher their chances of living longer. Importantly, Brodaty says, their chances of maintaining good lifetime cognition were higher, too.

"Eating a diet that's rich in vegetables, legumes, extra virgin olive oil, fish, lesser amounts of red meat and sweets, lesser amounts of processed food, watching their blood pressure and getting it checked and treated if it's high," were the best practices, Brodaty said.

Keeping socially connected and having purpose in life were also important. People who live longer "have something that drives them to live and feel valued".

Importantly, Brodaty said there were many simple ways to reduce your chances of getting dementia by almost half.

"We cannot smoke; we can avoid head injury if we can, avoid or treat diabetes. We know that people who have more exposure to green spaces and blue spaces also have a lower rate of dementia," Brodaty said.

"Eating well, remaining socially connected, keeping our brains active, using our brains, being physically active. Exercise is one of the best things we can do for our health in multiple ways."

Living longer, but at what cost?

But the comparison between Australia and Japan can only go so far, Brodaty said.

"We have to consider the demography of the two countries. Australia has 26,270,000 people. Japan has over 100,000,000 people."

Japan's long-lived, ageing population underscores a severe demographic crisis. It's part of the reason the number of centenarians seems "distorted", Brodaty said.

Japan has had a dwindling birth rate and ageing population for decades.

"This is really quite a crisis for Japan economically, because the number of people of working age, proportionately, is decreasing, and the number of people of working age who can look after older people is shrinking."

In Japan, there are roughly two working-age people for every elderly person aged 65 or older.

"Imagine that if we have only one person of working age to help support every older person," Brodaty asked. "How could we possibly arrange our society to deal with that?"

Brodaty said that while this would be an increasing crisis, there was a way to avert it.

"That is to try to help people live their lifespan healthily," he said. "So we talk about healthspan and lifespan, and that gap is what we're trying to narrow."

title: German chancellor declares AfD state election win 'a disaster'
text:
In brief The far-right AfD secured its latest state-level election win in eastern Germany.

The result puts fresh pressure on German Chancellor Friedrich Merz as his party suffers a historic setback.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has won state elections in north-east Germany, delivering the worst result for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative party since 1949.

"It's a disaster," Merz said after exit polls were published on Monday, but signalled he would fight on as chancellor and continue his reform agenda, despite speculation that a bad result could prompt him to resign.

The AfD was set to win 37 per cent in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, ahead of the centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) on 35.5 per cent and far in front of Merz’s conservatives, who got 5.5 per cent and barely crossed the threshold to enter the state parliament, according to exit polls on ARD public television.

Sunday's result looks set to deliver another first-place finish at the state level in a month for the AfD party, which tops national opinion polls but has been kept out of power by the other main parties' refusal to work with it.

In another election in the capital, Berlin, which also took place on Sunday, the far-left Die Linke party was at 24.5 per cent, while Merz's conservatives were at 20 per cent.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The AfD also gained in strength in the liberal city, hitting 16 per cent. It is the first time the Linke topped polls in the state, where it wants to nationalise housing from corporate landlords and cap rents.

The elections in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, a largely rural state in the formerly communist east, and in the capital, Berlin, follow the 6 September election in Saxony-Anhalt, where the AfD came close to the rare feat of winning an absolute majority.

Elections in the two states would not usually draw much interest outside Germany, but the AfD's success in Saxony-Anhalt, which it sees as the first step towards winning federal elections due in 2029, has sent shock waves through Europe.

In just over a decade, the party, which wants to take tough action to deport foreigners with no right to stay in Germany, restore energy ties with Russia, and quit the euro, has transformed itself from a fringe eurosceptic movement into the country's most popular party.

The exit polls underscore the advances the AfD has made in recent years and raise fresh questions over the "firewall" strategy, under which the other main parties refuse to enter coalition agreements with it.

Merz has struggled

Elected last year on a promise of reforms to return Germany's stagnant economy to growth, Merz has struggled to win over voters, compounding resentment over unpopular pension, tax and healthcare reforms with a stream of communication missteps.

Disillusion with his government has hung over the campaigns in both Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, where voters have focused on issues including soaring energy and housing costs. Merz presented a consumer relief package on Friday that included tax cuts on gas and diesel.

Several people who voted in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania said living costs were a major concern.

"Here in Schwerin, with these wages, you can hardly afford anything anymore," voter Carlotta Heick told Reuters in the state capital.

One elderly man criticised funding for foreign aid.

title: Motor neurone disease rates are rising. This new clinic hopes to stop it at the start
text:
In Brief The Brain Institute and Clinic will bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease.

MND impacts the brain and neurons that control muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

As the rates of a once-rare neurological disease rise, it is hoped that Australia's first combined institute and clinic focused on brain diseases will help find an effective treatment.

On Monday, Macquarie University will launch its Brain Institute and Clinic to bring together researchers and clinicians who specialise in motor neurone disease (MND) to understand its origins and how to treat it.

MND impacts parts of a person's brain and neurons that control their muscles, leading to progressive weakness and eventual paralysis.

It can affect adults of any age and most cases are not genetic.

Macquarie University deputy vice-chancellor Patrick McNeil noted there was still no effective cure for the deadly disease, despite it becoming increasingly common.

The purpose of the institute was to find treatments and deliver them to patients more quickly, he said.

"It typically takes an average of 17 years between when an important research discovery is made ... and when that is implemented in the clinic," McNeill told the Australian Associated Press.

"When you have integrated research and clinical institutions, that journey is shortened."

READ MORE I was researching motor neurone disease, then I was diagnosed with it myself

Earlier this month, NSW became the first jurisdiction in the world to make MND notifiable, meaning medical professionals are now legally required to report cases to the government.

McNeil said he hoped the decision would help researchers better understand the cause.

"It would be good if the other states follow because that is the way that you can find if there is an environmental agent," he said.

"Because what we have been seeing anecdotally is these clusters of cases that seem to be more frequent in a particular town or region than you would expect."

Dominic Rowe, who heads up Macquarie's Neurology Clinic, said 800 Australians would die from the disease this year.

"But I actually disagree with using the term die; motor neuron disease kills you," he said.

"We need to redouble our efforts into working out why so we can fix it."

The facility will also do research and treatment around Parkinson's disease and dementia, including Alzheimer's disease.

READ MORE Want to reduce your dementia risk? Lifestyle changes are only part of the picture

Macquarie University professor James Burrell said he was hopeful experts could build on recent breakthroughs in dementia treatment.

He said there were therapies available that slowed the physical progression of dementia caused by Alzheimer's.

"We now have disease-modifying therapies for this disease, and this gives me tremendous hope that we can identify disease-modifying therapies for other neurodegenerative diseases as well," Burrell said.

title: China's 13-year-old swimming prodigy Yu Zidi makes waves at Asian Games

title: Why Pauline Hanson joined forces with Muslim and Vietnamese-born MPs
text:
In brief Pauline Hanson, Fatima Payman and Dai Le have united to argue parliamentary staffing allocations are unfair.

The prime minister has significant discretion over personal staff, but the trio wants an independent system instead.

Pauline Hanson and Fatima Payman have clashed over race, religion and politics.

But this week, the One Nation leader and Muslim independent senator stood together, alongside Vietnamese-born independent MP Dai Le.

At the centre of their unlikely alliance is a fight over parliamentary staffing, with the three accusing Prime Minister Anthony Albanese of unfairly determining who gets additional staff and calling for the system to be taken out of the prime minister's hands.

The unlikely trio appeared together at Parliament House on Thursday, arguing the way personal staff are allocated to politicians is unfair and lacks transparency.

Their grievance centres on an unusual feature of Australia's parliamentary system: while MPs and senators employ their own staff, the prime minister has significant discretion over the allocation of additional personal staff.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

That discretion has previously faced scrutiny in parliament.

Why did Hanson, Payman and Le join forces?

Despite their political differences, all three say they are being denied the staffing resources they need to do their jobs adequately.

Payman, who left Labor in 2024 after crossing the Senate floor over Palestinian statehood, currently has no additional personal staff allocated to her.

Le, who defeated Labor to win the western Sydney seat of Fowler as an independent in 2022, has one.

One Nation, meanwhile, increased its representation at the 2025 election but says its staffing allocation did not increase accordingly.

According to the Australian Associated Press, modelling puts One Nation's allocation at 0.83 personal staff per parliamentarian, compared with 4.09 for Labor and 1.47 for the Coalition.

READ MORE Political leaders condemn Pauline Hanson over resurfaced remarks about Indigenous culture

Those figures include different categories of parliamentarians and office-holders, so they are not a direct like-for-like comparison of backbench MPs.

Hanson, Payman and Le argue the differences demonstrate the need for a more transparent and independent system.

According to The Conversation, Le told reporters on Thursday there were "no published criteria, no explanation, no appeal" for staffing decisions.

The three have threatened to pursue legislative changes when parliament returns in October to remove the prime minister's power over non-government personal staff allocations and give the responsibility to an independent authority.

Who actually decides how many staff politicians get?

Parliamentary staffing is divided into different categories, with different rules governing how positions are allocated.

Politicians generally have two broad categories of staff: electoral staff and personal staff.

Electorate staff perform work such as assisting constituents and supporting MPs and senators in their parliamentary duties.

Personal staff can perform different roles, including providing policy advice, research, communications and support for a parliamentarian's work in Canberra.

They are employed under the Members of Parliament (Staff) Act, commonly known as the MOP(S) Act, and cannot legally be employed for party-political purposes.

But additional personal staff are not distributed to every politician according to a single automatic formula.

The Department of Finance says the prime minister determines the number of personal employee positions allocated to ministers and assistant ministers, as well as the allocation given to the Opposition.

The prime minister also determines the allocation given to the leader of a minority party, who can then distribute those positions among their party's MPs, and may allocate personal staff to independent parliamentarians.

That means gaining another MP or senator does not necessarily translate into an increase in personal staff members.

Albanese's power over staff members is not unique. The system has given successive prime ministers significant control over personal staffing allocations

Why do extra staff matter?

Additional personal staff provide support across a range of parliamentary duties, and can affect their capacity to carry out parliamentary and electorate work.

They can research legislation, prepare MPs and senators for parliamentary debates and committee hearings, develop policy advice, deal with media and stakeholders and help offices manage correspondence and constituent issues.

Crossbenchers and smaller parties also have fewer parliamentary colleagues and party resources to draw on than the major parties.

READ MORE Dai Le thought she would die on her journey to Australia. She wants it to be easier for others to get here

The Parliamentary Library has previously noted that staffing levels for crossbenchers have varied significantly over time, and have sometimes changed depending on the political circumstances of the parliament.

When independents held the balance of power following the 2010 election, for example, additional staff were allocated to crossbench MPs. Those arrangements changed after the 2013 election.

Additional personal staff can assist parliamentarians with work including scrutinising legislation, preparing for parliamentary debates and participating in committee work.

Has this fight happened before?

The allocation of personal staff to crossbench parliamentarians has previously been contested, including since the Albanese government took office in 2022.

After Labor took office four years ago, Albanese reduced the number of additional personal staff allocated to crossbench parliamentarians, prompting significant criticism from independents.

A Parliamentary Library research paper subsequently noted that while the overall number of personal staff had increased substantially over the longer term, allocations to crossbenchers and former leaders had not increased in the same way.

The issue returned to parliament in 2025, when senators sought to change how personal staff were allocated to non-government parliamentarians and reduce the prime minister's discretion over the process.

A bill co-sponsored by Coalition and crossbench senators, including Hanson and Payman, proposed guaranteeing minimum personal staffing levels for non-government parliamentarians.

It also sought to limit the prime minister's discretion over those minimum allocations.

The bill passed its second reading in the Senate but was ultimately defeated at the third-reading stage in September 2025.

The Senate nevertheless backed an amendment calling for the government to work with elected groups and independents to develop a "fair and independent staffing model" that accounted for representation, staff wellbeing and workloads.

Reviews of parliamentary workplaces have also previously recommended greater transparency around staffing allocations and an evidence-based examination of workloads.

Why is their alliance so unusual?

Hanson and Payman, in particular, have a long history of clashing politically.

In 2024, Hanson sought to have Payman's eligibility to sit in parliament investigated over questions surrounding her Afghan citizenship.

Payman responded with a fierce attack on Hanson in the Senate, comments she was subsequently required to withdraw.

The political tensions between them remained.

Payman told reporters on Thursday, however, that politicians should be able to set those disagreements aside when they find a common cause, according to The Guardian.

title: Australia wants a seat at the UN's most powerful table. What power would it yield?
text:
IN BRIEF Australia is campaigning for a seat on the UN body responsible for international peace and security.

A seat would give Australia a vote and role in key negotiations, but not the veto held by five permanent members.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is heading to New York with a diplomatic pitch that has been more than a decade in the making: Putting Australia back on the United Nations Security Council.

Australia is campaigning for a non-permanent seat on the council for 2029-30, which would mark its first stint on the powerful UN body since 2014.

The government says a seat would give Australia a stronger voice on decisions affecting the country and the region.

Australia's campaign is expected to focus on issues including artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety, as well as climate action, international law and support for Pacific nations.

But what exactly does the UN Security Council do, and what would Australia gain by being on it?

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is the UN Security Council?

The Security Council is one of the six main bodies of the United Nations and has primary responsibility for maintaining international peace and security.

It is made up of 15 countries, each with one vote.

Five of them — China, France, Russia, the United Kingdom and the United States — are permanent members, while another 10 countries are elected by the UN General Assembly to serve two-year terms.

Unlike most other UN bodies, the Security Council can make decisions that member states are obligated to implement.

READ MORE We came to meet Tim Cook, but left with just a few photos

It can impose sanctions, establish peacekeeping operations and, in some circumstances, authorise the use of force. It can also investigate disputes, call for peaceful settlements and make recommendations aimed at maintaining or restoring international peace and security.

For a substantive resolution to pass, it needs at least nine votes.

And there is an important catch — each of the five permanent members has veto power, meaning a negative vote from any one of them can block a substantive resolution even if it otherwise has enough support.

Australia would not gain that veto power if elected, as it belongs exclusively to the five permanent members of the Security Council.

Non-permanent members such as Australia have the same single vote on council decisions, but cannot unilaterally block a substantive resolution.

What would Australia gain?

While a non-permanent seat does not come with a veto, it gives countries a direct role in decisions they would otherwise largely have to influence from outside the council.

Australia would have a vote on Security Council decisions and be involved in negotiating resolutions and other outcomes on conflicts and security crises around the world.

It would also take part in closed meetings and consultations between council members and could chair subsidiary bodies, including sanctions committees.

Every member also takes a turn holding the presidency of the Security Council for one calendar month, allowing them to preside over meetings and help shape the council's program of work.

Australia's previous term shows the practical difference membership can make.

During 2013-14, Australia participated in hundreds of council meetings, including closed meetings available only to members, and was closely involved in negotiating dozens of resolutions and presidential statements.

Its seat became particularly significant following the downing of Malaysia Airlines flight MH17 over eastern Ukraine in July 2014, which killed 298 people, including 38 Australian citizens and residents.

Australia authored and led negotiations on Security Council Resolution 2166, which was unanimously adopted four days after the crash.

The resolution condemned the downing of the plane, called for a full and independent investigation and demanded access to the crash site.

Australia also used its term to work on humanitarian access in Syria, counter-terrorism, small arms and the protection of civilians.

Why does Australia want a seat again?

The government argues that Australia's security and prosperity depend on an international system in which countries follow agreed rules and work collectively on global problems.

Foreign Minister Penny Wong has said a seat would give Australia "a stronger voice in the decisions that affect us and our region", describing the country as an active middle power with a role to play in international peace and security.

The bid is also increasingly focused on what Australia argues will be emerging security challenges by the time it takes up the seat.

Technology is expected to be central to the campaign, with the government arguing that artificial intelligence, cyber threats and online safety will increasingly intersect with international peace and security.

Speaking at a Security Council debate last year, Wong said AI had the potential to transform conflict and diplomacy and argued the council should play a role in developing international rules and norms around its use.

She said Australia's experience in digital infrastructure and technology partnerships would form part of what it could bring to the council.

Australia's broader foreign policy priorities, including the Pacific, climate change, protecting civilians and supporting international law, are also expected to feature in the campaign.

How does Australia get elected?

Australia cannot simply nominate itself and take a seat.

The 10 non-permanent positions are distributed between regional groupings, with five seats coming up for election each year.

Australia belongs to the Western European and Others Group, or WEOG, and is seeking one of the group's two seats available for the 2029-30 term.

So far, Australia and Finland are the only candidates for those two positions, meaning the positions are currently uncontested.

But Australia must still win the support of two-thirds of UN General Assembly members present and voting when the election is held in June 2028.

If all 193 UN member states were present and voted, that would mean securing around 129 votes.

It helps explain why the government is campaigning years before Australia would actually take its seat.

The bid itself is not new. It was first announced in 2015 under the former Coalition government, following Australia's previous stint on the council.

Australia has served five terms on the Security Council since the UN was established, most recently in 2013-14.

A sixth term would not give Australia the power enjoyed by the council's five permanent members.

But for two years, it would give Australia something it otherwise does not have: a seat, a vote and a direct role in negotiations at the UN body responsible for some of the world's most consequential decisions on peace and security.

title: John Farnham to skip tribute concert amid worsening health, family says
text:
In brief Australian and international music stars are due to perform at a John Farnham tribute concert.

Farnham would have loved to attend a tribute concert in his honour, his family says.

John Farnham's tribute concert will go ahead without him as the Australian music legend's family reveals his health has deteriorated.

The music-industry giant will be honoured by local and international performing greats at a blockbuster charity gig at Melbourne's Rod Laver Arena on Sunday, raising funds for the cancer support services that helped him through his own battle with the disease.

The 77-year-old, who has undergone several surgeries for oral cancer, now requires continuous oxygen support and 24-hour care.

A day before the sold-out event, Farnham's wife Jill and the couple's sons Robert and James, said they were "deeply moved by everything happening" at Rod Laver Arena.

"John's health has deteriorated in recent months," read a family statement posted to social media.

Advance Metals’ recent diamond core drilling has bored through a bonanza-grade one-metre intercept grading an eye-watering 4120 grams per tonne (g/t) silver at its flagship Gavilanes project in Mexico. The result came from just 66.7m depth downhole and formed part of a broader 4.6-metre intercept assaying an impressive 945g/t silver, 1.4 per cent zinc and one per cent lead. The result represents the highest ever individual silver assay returned from Advance’s drilling program at Gavilanes. The hole was designed to test for extensions below a high-grade hit in a recently drilled diamond hole and has successfully extended mineralisation, which remains open at depth and to the southwest. Cut diamond drill core from the headline hole, from 102.7 to 103.0m downhole depth, showing semi-massive coarse-grained lead sulphide (grey), with zinc sulphide (pale yellow), minor copper sulphide (bright yellow) and quartz (white). Adding another layer of potential value, the same hole also delivered the project’s most significant high-grade zinc-lead intersection encountered to date. A deeper 12-metre zone from 98.5m assayed 21g/t silver, 3.8 per cent zinc and 3.7 per cent lead. The interval also included a richer 5.3-metre core going 36g/t silver, 7.7 per cent zinc and 6.3 per cent lead from 102.7m. The results point to an expanding polymetallic system at Gavilanes, which lies just 23 kilometres from First Majestic Silver’s world-class San Dimas mine in Mexico’s silver-rich Sierra Madre Occidental Volcanic Belt. That operation has so far produced a massive 745 million ounces of silver and 11 million ounces of gold.

‘The drilling to date has identified high grade silver together with gold, copper, zinc and lead mineralisation.’ Advance Metals managing director and chief executive officer Dr Adam McKinnon First Majestic’s 2024 technical report on its resource and reserve estimates identified more than 125 mineralised quartz veins across its San Dimas property, with the silver and gold-rich quartz veins traced underground for strike lengths ranging from just a few metres to more than 1.5 kilometres. Advance Metals managing director and chief executive officer Dr Adam McKinnon said: “At over 4,000g/t silver, GV-26-008 returned the highest individual silver assay grade in Advance’s program to date and one of the best recorded at the project. The hole also returned the highest grade zinc-lead interval encountered at the Project to date, including 5.3 metres at 14% Zn+Pb - highlighting the potential for significant base metal credits as the mineralised footprint grows.” While silver remains the headline act, recent drilling to the south has also started to outline gold-dominant potential. Three drill holes have all returned gold-focused intersections, with a best result of 2.4m at 2.0g/t gold, 21g/t silver, 1.2 per cent zinc and 2.2 per cent lead from a shallow 14.4m. The company’s latest successes appear well timed, with Mexico’s long-running mining permitting logjam finally beginning to loosen under President Claudia Sheinbaum.

According to Mexican mining industry body CAMIMEX, the country’s Economy Ministry has now cleared more than 90 per cent of the mining permits within its remit, while environmental authority Semarnat has approved more than 85 per cent of its backlog. The shift is significant for a sector that only last month estimated some US$11 billion (A$15.5 billion) of potential mining investment was being held up by outstanding approvals. There is, however, an important wrinkle in Mexico’s improving regulatory story. While the permitting door is swinging open for companies that already hold mining concessions, securing brand-new exploration ground remains another matter. Mexico stopped granting new concessions in 2019 and the Sheinbaum administration has continued to take a cautious approach to opening fresh ground. The change therefore looks more like a controlled thaw than a wholesale reopening of Mexico’s mining sector, with the government clearing bureaucratic bottlenecks around existing projects while retaining tighter control over new concessions. Not that the distinction should trouble Advance at its key Mexican projects. Its Gavilanes project already comprises 11 mining concessions covering 136 square kilometres and a further seven concessions at its 100%-owned Yoquivo silver project in Chihuahua, all in good standing. Advance’s maiden drilling program at its 136-square-kilometre project is squarely aimed at growing and converting the project’s existing foreign resource estimate of 2.83 million tonnes at 246g/t silver equivalent for 22.4 million ounces.
