Smith did perhaps the quickest change in Brownlow history, throwing on his unique interpretation of black tie, which would have looked more at home in a ’70s flick, in what appeared in a social media clip to be a function room on the same level as the Crown Palladium ballroom where the medal count was taking place.

Advertisement

All eyes were watching the quirky Cat when he appeared at his table and, frankly, he was impossible to ignore. Turns out the suit was a vehicle to advertise his ready-to-drink booze brand, Barry, with the lining featuring the brand’s logo – as an ambush-marketing flex, it was not subtle. A pair of silver, surfer sunnies and a sling to support his recently operated-on right shoulder, were a vibe of their own. Geelong star Bailey Smith arrives at the 2026 Brownlow Medal 2½ hours late in a tracksuit. @bazlenka/Instagram Seated alongside Patrick Dangerfield on the Geelong table, Smith’s look became progressively more casual as the night wore on – his bow tie disappeared, the top buttons of his shirt were undone.

Advertisement

In the room, it was hard to escape the notion that were other places Smith would have preferred to be. Related Article Brownlow Medal Brownlow Medal 2026 red carpet as it happened: Best fashion looks and biggest moments It was widely talked about among guests that he had tried to pull out of attending, and been a little hard to get a hold of, after his reconstructive surgery a little over a week ago for a chronic complaint that he had carried all season. But another theory for his distraction was said to be a budding romance that had recently gone south. We will take that on notice given Smith’s social calendar is a challenge to keep track of, but either way, we hope the off-season is kind to the dynamic player.

Advertisement

If this year’s count is anything to go by, the umpires are a fan of his work, and CBD would love nothing more than to see him collect a Brownlow in the not-too-distant future. Hirdy’s sparkling introduction to his new partner Essendon great James Hird ripped the Band-Aid off his marriage break-up by debuting his new partner, Natalie Young. The pair have been seeing each other for “a while”, but attending the Brownlow was a good old-fashioned hard launch as a couple. James Hird and Natalie Young at the 2026 Brownlow Medal. via Getty Images

Advertisement

Hird, who quietly split from his wife of 27 years, Tania, in 2024, won the Brownlow in 1996. Monday’s count was his first since 2012 when Essendon’s Jobe Watson won but handed back in 2016 due to Essendon’s controversial supplements program. Hird and Young, who it is understood has worked in recruitment, fashion and property, were seated on a table with former Brownlow Medal winners including Shane Crawford, Ben Cousins and Simon Black. Related Article Brownlow Medal Nude illusion and 90s throwbacks: The Brownlow red carpet fashion winners and sinners Young’s sparkling red dress made her an instant red carpet favourite, posing for photos with Hird and happily submitting to requests from photographers and cameramen for the footy great to give her a twirl to show off the backless gown. Legal elephant in the room

Advertisement

Taking a stroll between the tables during a break in proceedings, CBD came across legal eagle Tony Carbone, of Carbone Lawyers, holding court among the Brownlow guests. Talk about the elephant in the room. Carbone’s firm is representing two of the women who have claimed they were sexually assaulted at the Pullman East Melbourne hotel in August. Five Sydney Swans players, Isaac Heeney, Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Nick Blakey and James Jordon, were involved some after-hours antics at the Pullman that saw their club disgraced and them banned from playing and attending the medal night. Four of the players are the subject of an ongoing police investigation, with Bice having been cleared of any criminal wrongdoing. No one has been charged in relation to the incident. Conveniently, Carbone’s table and the one hosting the slimmed-down Swans’ contingent that had travelled to Melbourne for the evening, were on opposite sides of the Crown Palladium ballroom. The top table

Advertisement

Next up, CBD had a look at who was perched on AFL commissioner Craig Drummond’s table – the seats of power in the room. Joining Drummond and his wife when we swung past were Sports Minister Steve Dimopoulos, Foxtel Group chief executive Peter O’Connell, chair of Tourism Australia and the Herald & Weekly Times Penny Fowler, John Lehmann, News Corp Australia’s managing director for Victoria and Tasmania, Toyota’s John Pappas, and Brian Walsh, the executive director of the Foxtel Group. Jess Wilson with Nick and Josh Daicos at the 2026 Brownlow Medal. @jesswilsonmp/instagram It clearly helps to get a table at the front of the room if you’ve got an expensive broadcast deal with the AFL. Finally, Opposition Leader Jess Wilson showed her true colours on Monday. The mad Magpies supporter not only nabbed a selfie with man of the moment, Nick Daicos, and his brother Josh, but was also spotted during the evening introducing Liberal colleague Brad Battin to the pair.

SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby New Zealand to consider walking away from Super Rugby at major summit Iain Payten September 22, 2026 — 1:38pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

New Zealand will consider walking away from Super Rugby Pacific and Australia, and replacing the 30-year-old competition with a new 8-10 team domestic league. The “bombshell proposal”, which was revealed by the Wellington-based Post newspaper on Tuesday, is one of three options contained in a secret document provided to stakeholders ahead of a major New Zealand Rugby summit on Thursday. Loading The summit, which will see 80 executives from NZR, Super Rugby clubs, provincial unions and the NZ Players Association gather in Wellington, comes as NZR grapples with ways to avoid a looming financial crisis. It was revealed last week in another secret pre-summit document that the NZR are facing losses of $53 million between 2027-2031, even after the massive windfall of a Lions tour in 2029.

Advertisement

With a “structural deficit” of about $16m a year, NZR is searching for ways to cut costs, and one key area of discussion at the summit will be the future of men’s elite competitions. New Zealand runs five Super Rugby teams and 14 National Provincial Championship teams. The NZR document proposes three options for discussion: replacing Super Rugby and the NPC with a domestic professional competition; expanding Super Rugby by two more teams; or continuing Super Rugby and the NPC but with Super and NPC entities combined in Auckland, Waikato, Wellington, Canterbury and Otago. The Crusaders could become part of a domestic New Zealand competition, under a proposal to be dicusssed at a New Zealand summit. Getty Images The option to walk away from Australia and Fiji and go it alone is the most explosive item on the agenda, and informed sources with knowledge of the matter said it was put into the document by the 26 provincial unions, who all get a vote as NZR members and are hugely powerful. The Post reported that the proposal spells out the eight to 10 teams in a national competition would receive up to $8m for player payments and be run by provincial unions. It would open the door for private investment as well, the report said.

Advertisement

Related Article Analysis

Rugby Australia Forget the romance. Rugby Australia and NZ Rugby are locked in a marriage of necessity Rugby Australia declined to comment on the Post’s report and a potential exit from Super Rugby by the Kiwi sides. But informed sources with knowledge of both unions said the NZR leadership has made it clear to RA as recently as this week that they remain committed to the trans-Tasman relationship, and to playing in Super Rugby Pacific. The NZR and RA are one year into a five-year broadcast deal for Super Rugby Pacific, and recent discussions between the two unions have covered the possibility of a 10-team competition expanding into Japan and the US. But the expansion to be discussed as an option at the NZR summit is adding two extra teams in New Zealand, presumably from two of the stronger provinces. The document says this option would require “Rugby Australia agreement”, according to the Post. The option to combine the five New Zealand Super Rugby clubs with the provincial unions based in their city would help generate significant savings by eliminating some duplication. The NZR summit, which is an annual event, will consider all proposals before a final position is put to the NZR board in December.

title: Russel’s life changed when he hit a pothole. Now, he’s part of a growing wave of litigation
text:
Advertisement

NationalVictoriaRoad safety Russel’s life changed when he hit a pothole. Now, he’s part of a growing wave of litigation Alexander Darling September 22, 2026 — 12:17pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Boxing Day 2022 was turning into a great day for Russel Heggen. As he cruised along Arthurs Seat Road on his Harley-Davidson, the bay spread out before him as he snaked his way back towards his Dromana home. The then 62-year-old didn’t even see the pothole before he hit it. The patch of road had recently been repaired, but Heggen claims the tar had become misshapen with cars driving over it, making a mound at one end and effectively turning it into a ramp. Russel Heggen has filed a personal injury lawsuit against the Department of Transport. He claims the road surface forced him to come off his motorbike on Arthurs Seat Road in 2022. Jason South The impact caused Heggen to involuntarily tighten his grip on the throttle, and he and his Harley went off the road, flying between two trees and off a cliff. Emergency services estimate he travelled 15 metres, but his memory of the crash is fuzzy.

Advertisement

“I was just very lucky to survive,” he said. Luck aside, Heggen was seriously injured, suffering a broken femur and tibia, a fractured pelvis and spine, a collapsed lung and a brain injury. The patched pothole on Arthurs Seat Road that Heggen said acted as a ramp for his motorbike. The ordeal is now detailed in a writ before the Supreme Court, with the 66-year-old joining a growing number of Victorians making public liability claims against road authorities for the serious injuries sustained after accidents allegedly caused by poor road surfaces. In the vast majority of cases, the Transport Accident Commission covers medical expenses related to road accidents. However, under Victorian law, in rare circumstances, road authorities – state and local governments – can be held liable for injuries.

Advertisement

The condition of Victoria’s roads, particularly in regional and rural areas, has become a hot-button issue in the lead-up to the November 28 state election. Concerns boiled over earlier this month when Ballarat motorcyclist Peter “Tiki” Mason, 71, died on the Western Highway after his bike hit a pothole. Several personal injury law firms spoken to by The Age said they had had an increase in inquiries from people wanting compensation for pothole-related road accidents. Peter Mason died on September 14 after his motorcycle hit a pothole on the Western Highway near Ballarat. Facebook, Joe Armao “It’s a wave that’s coming,” Henry Carus, head of Henry Carus & Associates, said. “I think people will get injured while taking evasive action just because of the size of the holes,” he said, noting his firm is overseeing a claim against South Gippsland Shire Council involving a motorcyclist who lost control after hitting a pothole.

Advertisement

Law firm Arnold Thomas & Becker has begun action against Northern Grampians Shire Council on behalf of a woman who suffered several fractures and a torn artery when she lost control of her car near Stawell. Related Series

Victorian election Victoria’s pothole crisis In each case, the lawsuits accuse the respective councils of a litany of failings, including “failing to adequately inspect, maintain, repair or warn road users” about the dangers of the roads in question – the same wording as Heggen’s claim against the Department of Transport. Any recompense the plaintiffs receive as a result of these lawsuits will be in addition to TAC compensation, which all victims of road crashes are entitled to regardless of who is at fault. The existence of a pothole or poor road surface is not enough on its own to prove liability for road authorities. Plaintiffs must be able to prove authorities knew of the threat a section of road posed at the time it caused an accident, and failed to address it appropriately.

Advertisement

In Heggen’s case, his wife, Amanda, and son Mitch took photos of the offending pothole on the same day as the accident. These images are included in the writ for his court action and show a clear mound of road surfacing material sitting several centimetres higher at one edge of the repaired area. Amanda said this turned out to be crucial when her husband eventually decided in 2025 to pursue legal action after receiving less compensation from the TAC than other road crash victims. Heggen about to be flown to The Alfred hospital on the day of the accident. Amanda Heggen “Our lawyers said, ‘That’s all you’re entitled to under the guidelines because no one is at fault’,” she said. “The lawyers said only a few negligence claims had been successful, and they had all had photos and videos, which I gave to them.”

Advertisement

But even a claim with evidence has no certainty of success. Last week, the Supreme Court ruled against a motorcyclist who had been injured the day before Heggen in 2022, on a stretch of road in Reedy Creek, 100 kilometres north of Melbourne. Joshua Masters claimed he lost control of his motorbike after swerving to avoid a pothole and poorly repaired road. But Justice Andrew Keogh concluded Masters had not proved the road authority, in this case Mitchell Shire Council, was liable for the accident. Keogh ruled that while the council had been aware of the defect and inspected it in a careless manner, the road was below the threshold for intervention.

Advertisement

Heggen says he has lost his easy-going nature since the accident and becomes anxious more easily, though he is trying his best to stay positive. Though the writ for Heggen’s case was issued in June, he has been advised it won’t be heard before August 2027. In the meantime, the lifelong member of the Dromana Football Club continues physiotherapy and pool rehabilitation. His wife has also helped by reorganising the layout of their home to assist him, and devising strategies to accommodate his short-term memory issues. “I’m lucky Russel’s resilient. He works with me and never complains about pain,” she said.

Advertisement

Amanda says that pursuing legal action is in part about seeking compensation for Russel’s recovery, but is also about vindication. “At the start of this, Russ said to me all he wanted was someone to acknowledge it was the road surface that caused the incident,” she said. “It’s an issue of public safety. We’re really hopeful that this court case leads to more funding available to fix the root cause of the problem, rather than the government compensating people afterwards.” A Department of Transport spokesperson declined to comment on Heggen’s case as it is before the courts. “Speed, driver fatigue, distractions and a vehicle’s safety features remain the biggest contributors to serious injury crashes,” they said, noting more than 66,000 potholes had been repaired in recent months, with works set to increase to meet Premier Ben Carroll’s pledge of rectifying half a million of them.

title: Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making
text:

SportAFLBrownlow Medal Nike called Daicos’ Brownlow win ‘inevitable’. His new votes record was years in the making Marc McGowan Updated September 22, 2026 — 12:06pm ,first published September 21, 2026 — 10:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Nike was right – it was inevitable. After consecutive runner-up finishes, and a third placing before that, Collingwood champion Nick Daicos is finally a Brownlow medallist. Nick Daicos (right) with his parents Peter and Colleen. AFL Photos Daicos’ major sponsor Nike boldly took out front-page newspaper ads on Monday featuring a photo of the star Magpie, the famous swoosh logo, and the word “Inevitable”. The iconic brand’s confidence was vindicated when the 23-year-old midfielder, wearing custom swoosh cufflinks, won in record-breaking style, beating dual winner Patrick Cripps’ extraordinary 2024 tally of 45 votes with a new count-high total (in the 3-2-1 system) of 47.

Advertisement

The shortest-priced favourite in the event’s history also set a new benchmark of 13 best-on-ground performances and polled in 18 of his 22 matches. Daicos’ victory was sealed with three rounds to go – when he was 10 votes clear – and he eventually equalled Richmond legend Dustin Martin’s record winning margin of 11 votes from 2017, ending his multi-year run of being a beaten Brownlow favourite. “I’ve learnt not to trust the betting markets,” Daicos said after receiving his Brownlow Medal from last year’s winner and former Carey Grammar teammate Matt Rowell. “But, no, there is [relief]. It’s a massive award, and I’m so privileged to be up here. I can’t believe I’m a Brownlow medallist.”

Advertisement

Geelong superstar Bailey Smith (36 votes), Western Bulldogs captain Marcus Bontempelli (34), Melbourne skipper Max Gawn (28), North Melbourne’s Harry Sheezel, Blue Patrick Cripps and Brisbane’s dual North Smith medallist Will Ashcroft (27) finished behind Daicos. Sydney’s Isaac Heeney was a further vote back on 26 with Zak Butters, but was unable to attend the event after his role in the Pullman Hotel saga. Speaking during the count, Bontempelli said Daicos was the AFL’s best player and had changed the sport with his ability to impact the game with pure hard work and his offensive skills. View post on X

Advertisement

Daicos revealed post-count that his brother and teammate Josh and father Peter – one of Collingwood’s all-time greats – were instrumental in him developing his famed work ethic. Nick and Josh spent countless afternoons as teenagers with their dad at Greythorn Falcons honing their skills. “I feel like from a young age, I probably had more talent [than others] and didn’t work as hard, and had some chats with Dad and Josh as I grew up,” he said. “It was a realisation I wanted to play AFL, and that I needed to train harder. I walk into the club every day, and I’m immensely grateful to be an AFL footballer.

Advertisement

“I think I owe it to the Collingwood Football Club to train with an intensity, and I feel like as a leader at the club, I can’t ask the bloke next to me to put his backside on the line and train really hard if I’m not doing it myself. I try and lead by example.” Daicos’ custom Nike cufflinks. AFL Photos Daicos’ profile and ability to influence young, adoring fans isn’t lost on him, either. He used part of his acceptance speech to single out eight-year-old fan named Logan, who is battling cancer. “I worked closely with him this year, and I think that just shows the platform we can have in impacting people like that – we send videos back and forth throughout the week, and we’re only able to do that and put a smile on his face because we’re playing footy, but then at the same time I think he’s probably taught me more than I’ve taught him,” Daicos explained.

Advertisement

Growing up, footballs were banished from the house by Nick and Josh’s mother, Colleen, but the boys quickly found an alternative. “Dad was creative. He’d scrunch the toilet paper up into this little oval shape, and then we’d go to Officeworks, get some sticky tape, and wrap it the whole way around,” he said. “I think it worked for everyone because we weren’t getting the red marks on the wall, so Mum was happy, too.” Daicos’ Brownlow victory followed him also collecting the AFL Players’ Association’s MVP and AFL Coaches’ Association’s player of the year, becoming the first footballer to claim all three since Lachie Neale six years ago.

Advertisement

His latest honour makes him arguably the most accomplished young player ever, swelling a resume that already includes the Magpies’ 2023 premiership and four All-Australian selections. Daicos will almost certainly win a third Copeland Trophy next month as well. He is the 10th Magpie to win a Brownlow Medal and first since Dane Swan 15 years ago, also joining Syd Coventry, brothers Albert and Harry Collier, Marcus Whelan, Des Fothergill, Len Thompson, Peter Moore and Nathan Buckley. Daicos polled maximum votes in each of his first three games – either side of the Magpies’ round two bye – before he was a late withdrawal with a corked calf against Brisbane. That was the only match he missed all season.

Advertisement

Daicos proudly shows off the 2026 Brownlow Medal after a record-breaking night. AFL Photos Daicos’ streak of maximum votes ended in a round five loss to Fremantle, where he still polled one off a 31-disposal effort, and it was enough to break an early deadlock with fellow great Bontempelli. Zak Butters briefly snatched a one-vote lead in round 10, but Daicos was back on top a round later when he was best afield against West Coast as Scott Pendlebury broke the VFL/AFL games record with his 433rd appearance. Smith drew level with the gun Pie on 23 votes in round 14, with Butters a single vote back, before Daicos shot away again a round later with three votes after a 41-touch masterclass at Port Adelaide’s expense.

Advertisement

That was when Daicos made his move, turning an entertaining count with superstars spread across the leaderboard into a demolition, like a Melbourne Cup winner turning for home. The man in the No.35 secured maximum votes in six straight matches between rounds 15 and 20 in an incredible purple patch to kick clear of the field and end any doubt about the result. Daicos polled 11 votes to finish equal 27th in his debut season in 2022; came third with 28 votes in 2023; second with 38 votes in 2024; and second with 32 votes last year. Umpires had access to player statistics for the first time this year to help with voting.

title: QLD demerger frees Broken Hill for SA gold focus
text:

Sponsored BusinessCompaniesBulls N' Bears QLD demerger frees Broken Hill for SA gold focus Brought to you by BULLS N’ BEARS Penny Taylor September 22, 2026 — 12:06pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Broken Hill Gold has completed the strategic demerger of its North Queensland portfolio, transferring its Alice River gold and St George gold-antimony projects to Manda Resources. The deal clears the decks for an all-out focus on its White Dam gold operation in South Australia. The transaction hands Manda Broken Hill’s 100 per cent interest in Alice River and its St George earn-in rights for 64M Manda shares valued at $16M, plus $650,000 cash payable on Manda’s ASX admission. Subject to shareholder approval, all the shares, valued at 25 cents each, will be distributed in specie to eligible shareholders, retaining their exposure to the Queensland story. Under indicative terms announced in June, they would receive one Manda share for every 6.76 Broken Hill shares, with the final ratio set at the record date. Broken Hill Gold’s operational gold processing plant at White Dam in South Australia, now the company’s sole focus following its Queensland demerger. ASX-listed mining junior Emerald Resources has also brought heavyweight backing and a safe pair of hands to Manda. The company initially invested $6.4M into Manda’s $9M pre-IPO seed raising for a 49 per cent shareholding. It has since flagged another $4.25M investment in the initial public offering, which is expected to raise at least $21M, subject to market conditions. Emerald intends to maintain a 19.9 per cent Manda holding at listing. Manda has also wrapped up its acquisition of Territory Minerals, bringing the Tregoora, Northcote, Atric and Reedy gold projects under the same roof. Alice River contributes 26.8 million tonnes at 1.00 grams per tonne (g/t) gold for 854,000 ounces, while Territory adds 480,000 ounces, giving the portfolio 1.33 million ounces across more than 1700 square kilometres.

Advertisement

‘The demerger means we are now exceptionally well-positioned to execute on our focused strategy, with maiden production at White Dam achieved and cashflow from gold production imminent.’ Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes Manda has also strengthened its leadership, putting veteran exploration geologist Tara French at the helm as chief executive officer. French brings more than 25 years’ experience and was most recently Cazaly Resources’ managing director after serving as Regis Resources’ general manager, exploration. At Alice River, Manda inherits plenty to chase along a 30km prospective strike on the Alice River Fault Zone, part of a regional-scale intrusion-related system Broken Hill has compared geologically with globally significant gold systems Fort Knox in the United States and Hemi in Western Australia. Its nearby St George project adds a 905-square-kilometre gold-antimony footprint, where exploration has defined more than 20km of mineralised and geochemical strike, yet drilling has tested just 200m. That leaves plenty of room to build on early high-grade antimony and gold hits. Broken Hill Gold managing director Matthew Boyes said: “This strategic demerger is a highly compelling transaction. Having Emerald Resources’ management driving this new vehicle is a real endorsement of the geological potential at the Alice River and St George Projects. Manda’s concurrent acquisition of Territory Minerals will create a dominant explorer in a region with clear multimillion-ounce potential.”

Advertisement

Attention now turns to Manda’s listing. Its prospectus and Broken Hill’s notice of meeting are targeted for early November, with the shareholder vote due in early December and Manda’s targeted ASX admission in mid-December. Distributed shares are expected to face 12 months of mandatory escrow from their issue date. Back in South Australia, White Dam is now primed to take centre stage for Broken Hill. The project has more than 50 prospects, many lightly tested at depth, with more than 30,000m of reverse-circulation and diamond drilling planned over the next 18 months to probe its deeper gold-copper potential. The operation produced roughly 180,000 ounces between 2010 and 2018 and comes with open pits, heap-leach infrastructure and an operational gold extraction plant, giving the company a brownfields springboard rather than a standing-start development. The near-minegrounds span Vertigo and Hannaford alongside the emerging Icebreaker gold-copper discovery, with existing processing infrastructure providing a ready pathway for shallow oxide material. Its latest Vertigo update lifted White Dam’s global resource to 5.2 million tonnes at 0.7g/t gold for 118,496 ounces, including 24,300 indicated ounces at Vertigo. Mining studies will assess an oxide heap-leach restart, once the current material on the leach pad has been processed, with a prefeasibility study planned after the remaining shallow resources are drilled and updated.

Advertisement

Now, with two rigs in the field, Broken Hill can push ahead on shallow oxide drilling while accelerating the deeper sulphide hunt at Vertigo and Icebreaker. With the Queensland baton passed to Manda, Broken Hill’s gold pendulum has swung firmly south. At White Dam, the clock is already running on both a return to open-pit mining and the hunt for a deeper gold-copper prize. Is your ASX-listed company doing something interesting? title: ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us
text:
Advertisement

BusinessMarketsOil Opinion ‘Stop the bleeding’? A Trump move to stop the diesel spike could hurt all of us Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist September 22, 2026 — 12:04pm

September 22, 2026 — 12:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Trump White House is under mounting pressure to “do something” about the price of diesel in the US. That something would have dire consequences for much of the world, including the US – and Australia, the world’s biggest per-capita user of the fuel. A lengthening queue of Republicans, including Senate majority leader John Thune, have called for the US to consider banning or restricting exports of diesel after its average domestic price hit another record of $US6.51 ($9.14) a gallon on Monday. That’s about 75 per cent higher than the average US price a year ago. The price of diesel has smashed records, just weeks before the midterm elections. AP With farmers, who are about to start their autumn harvest season, the heartland constituency for Republicans, it isn’t surprising that their political representatives, mainly Republicans, are becoming anxious in the lead-up to November’s midterm elections. Where the White House initially waved off suggestions of limiting diesel exports, arguing – rightly – that it could be counter-productive, there have been signs recently that the attitude is thawing as the elections loom.

Advertisement

Donald Trump appears to be very aware of the political implications, but is misdiagnosing the cause of the big spike in prices. Related Article Analysis

Trump's White House Behind Trump’s bluster there’s a sobering realisation he is losing the public At the weekend, he repeated his call for Ukraine to stop its drone attacks on Russian refineries, almost all of which – with the exception of a handful of hard-to-reach plants in Siberia – have been damaged by Ukrainian bombing. “Russia has unfortunately lost control of its Diesel Oil Industry due to its War with Ukraine,” Trump posted on Truth Social. “A large number of their Diesel refineries have been blown up and are, at least temporarily, out of commission. This ridiculous and never-ending war with Ukraine must be ended.”

Advertisement

As a result of the Ukrainian attacks, Russia – a major exporter of diesel before its invasion of the country – has halted all exports and is now importing diesel, mainly from India. Related Article Exclusive

Blood Oil Funding Putin: ‘Blood oil’ imports from major Asian supplier surge While that is contributing to the surge in diesel prices globally, it isn’t the primary cause. Last year, Russia exported about 800,000 barrels a day of diesel and gas oil, making it the world’s second-largest exporter behind the US. The Middle East, as a region, however, exported about 1.5 million barrels a day. With those Middle Eastern exports now reduced by more than 50 per cent, it is Trump’s war on Iran that’s the major influence on the diesel shortages that are driving up prices.

Advertisement

It is Trump’s war on Iran that’s the major influence on the diesel shortages that are driving up prices. It hasn’t helped that China, a major processor of crude oil into distillates including diesel, halted exports earlier this year after the attacks on Iran. It subsequently resumed them but, with its inventories at their lowest level for more than a year, is expected to reintroduce export curbs. Moreover, unlike crude supply, where the end of hostilities in the Middle East would see a rapid rebound in supply, elevated diesel prices are likely to be a feature of the global markets for months after the war’s conclusion, if not years, because of the extensive damage to the region’s refineries. The same timelines would apply to Russia’s infrastructure if that war were to end. The Senate’s majority leader John Thune (left) is among the Republicans urging Trump to limit diesel exports. AP Photo/Jacquelyn Martin What US Republicans are urging the White House to do to “stop the bleeding” ranges from a complete ban on diesel exports to restrictions that link permitted exports to domestic diesel prices. There are also calls for the scrapping of fuel excises and financial subsidies for farmers and truckers.

Advertisement

An export ban would keep the diesel that the US currently exports within the US, but would have devastating consequences for those countries that have become increasingly reliant on America’s record exports since the war in the Middle East erupted. In Europe, where record prices are the equivalent of a $US190 a barrel oil price and inventories are at record lows for this time of the year, there are already supply shortages even before the region heads into the northern winter. Diesel-dependent Asia is just as vulnerable, if not more so. Related Article Exclusive

Energy Supply crunch hits Australian fuel distributors at east-coast ports But any restrictions in exports could have adverse consequences for the US itself, too. While it is the world’s largest diesel exporter, it does import about 165,000 barrels a day. That’s because much of its refining capacity is on the US Gulf Coast, with limited pipeline infrastructure to the north-east and west coasts. In any event, most of the pipelines linking refineries to their end markets are operating at or near capacity.

Advertisement

An export ban would see prices surge further in those regions which the infrastructure doesn’t reach, and lead to a build-up of inventories within the refineries. The US accounts for about 1.5 million barrels a day of the daily 8 million barrels or so of the global seaborne trade in diesel. A US export ban would see global prices soar further, with flow-on consequences for those US regions dependent on imported product. More broadly, with an export ban or restrictions, there’d be more diesel held within the US. But the refineries, which have been operating at close to full capacity, would reduce their crude oil purchases because they’d be physically incapable of delivering much more than they do today, let alone the 30 per cent or so increase in diesel supply required to absorb the diverted export volumes. Even a brief relief from high prices might save a few seats and help protect Trump from the inevitability of a lame-duck second half to his presidency Areas close to the refineries might get lower prices, but the rest of the country would probably experience even higher prices.

There’s also the problem that, unless crude oil prices fell sharply, refinery margins would be squeezed if diesel prices fell, likely leading to reduced, rather than increased, production. Refinery profits and export revenues would be lost and the refiners’ relationships with their offshore customers would be damaged, without any lasting benefit in the form of lower domestic prices. US politics At half-full stadium, Trump makes desperate pitch to save the midterms So, if both a total or partial ban on diesel exports are likely to be counter-productive, why would senior Republicans be forcing it onto the White House agenda? It’s the elections, of course, where control of the House, and perhaps even the Senate, is likely to be determined by cost-of-living issues, with gasoline and diesel prices front-of-mind with voters.

Diesel, because of the role it plays in transport, shipping and agriculture, is also a meaningful influence on the inflation rate. The longer prices remain at record levels, the more those prices are likely to feed into the elevated prices of food and consumer goods generally, forcing the inflation rate to remain high and increasing the likelihood of further rate hikes by the Federal Reserve, perhaps as early as next month – just weeks ahead of the midterms. It is apparent that there are some in the White House who are aware that, while a ban might cause an initial drop in the price of diesel, the reprieve would be temporary and the longer-term consequences would probably be damaging to the economy, businesses and consumers. title: ‘Nonsense’: Major racing club blames jockeys for track drama, dismisses safety concerns
text:
Advertisement

SportRacingVictorian racing ‘Nonsense’: Major racing club blames jockeys for track drama, dismisses safety concerns Danny Russell September 22, 2026 — 12:01pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Melbourne Racing Club has dismissed any concerns about track safety at Caulfield Racecourse, despite images of jockeys lifting large clumps of turf in the home straight before Saturday’s group 1 race meeting. The club released a strongly worded statement on Tuesday claiming the jockeys’ pre-race safety concerns were “nonsense”, and said a decision to move the running rail and delay the start of the meeting was unnecessary. A clod of dirt lifted from the Caulfield track before race one. Getty Images The MRC’s declaration that there was never any issue with the Caulfield surface comes in a week that they boasted of a record $281.4 million turnover in the past financial year despite suffering a $10.6 million loss. Saturday’s delay at Caulfield came after a group of jockeys identified loose “plugs” in sections of the track before the first event, leading stewards to order maintenance staff to make last-minute alterations.

Advertisement

Plugs are large, turf covered clumps of dirt that are wedged into divots to make them safe for horses to run over. MRC CEO Tanya Fullarton said an internal review “found no safety issue” with Saturday’s track. Caulfield track staff moved the running rail before Saturday’s meeting started. Getty Images “The turf plugs were correctly installed, the track as presented was safe for racing and the rail did not need to be moved,” Fullarton said. “The track subsequently raced safely and fairly throughout the meeting. Dozens of exactly the same turf plugs remained on other sections of the track that continued to be raced on after the rail movement, with no issues for jockeys and horses.

Advertisement

“The jockeys clearly did not understand how turf plugs work. The jockeys’ claim that being able to pull the tops off the plugs somehow showed that the track was unsafe is nonsense. “Turf plugs are routinely installed a few days before a race day and are always able to be physically pulled up, as grass plugs take at least two weeks to bind with the rest of the turf profile. “This has been standard practice for over 25 years and is not a problem – they remain in place while horses gallop over them, with no risk to jockeys or horses.” To avoid future issues, Racing Victoria has enlisted former champion jockey Damien Oliver to conduct independent track inspections for the next 12 weeks. Oliver will inspect the surface for this Sunday’s group 1 Manikato Stakes meeting at Caulfield, and will continue to do so throughout the spring, including all Flemington meetings.

Advertisement

Related Article Victorian racing Legal feuds, boardroom battles and a 24-year-old taking on racing’s elite He will report to Racing Victoria stewards before each race day starts to provide a safety assessment of the tracks. “Saturday showed the importance of ensuring any concerns about a racing surface are properly assessed, with the appropriate technical input, before significant decisions are made on race day,” Fullarton said. “The stewards were placed in an extremely difficult position, with concerns raised by jockeys less than an hour before the first race. “With the limited time available, they were unable to properly consult with our track team about the purpose, installation and condition of the plugs before making the incorrect decision to move the rail.

Advertisement

“Our track team complied with that direction so the meeting could proceed, but this is not how these issues should have to be dealt with on race day.” Despite the club dismissing any safety concerns, the rail will be moved out 13m for Sunday’s Manikato meeting, which has been transferred from Moonee Valley. “The reason the rail isn’t moving to the true position is to protect the track for the Caulfield Cup carnival,” a club spokesperson said. It is not the first time the MRC has come under fire from punters this year, following criticism for the standard of its tracks at Caulfield and Sandown during the winter months. On top of that, two barrier attendants were lucky to escape injury in June when starting barriers were accidentally reversed into a lake in the middle of Sandown Racecourse. They were later fished out with a crane.

Advertisement

“It would probably be a good idea for MRC to change their name back to VATC … Very Amateur Turf Club as the legend of racing writers used to refer to it,” prominent owner Nick Williams posted on X on Saturday. Jockey Patrick Moloney told Racing.com the track surface was fine after the pre-race alterations, but the changes had made it “really awkward” to navigate for riders. The MRC released its annual general report on Monday, revealing a second consecutive substantial loss, this year’s $10.6 million deficit following $14.7 million in the 2025 financial year. The club forked out $10.9 million in bank interest in the past year on $197.7 million in borrowings, which it said it expected to clear with the sale of land at Caulfield to Mount Scopus College for $195 million. The Jewish school signed an agreement to purchase the land in December 2024 and was given two years to exercise that option. The deal has still not been finalised.

Advertisement

The MRC now has 17 poker machine venues after recently buying two new outlets - The Cumberland and the Cheltenham Club - and these venues brought in $128.2 million last year and made a $48.3 million profit. Related Article Victorian racing Caulfield order track safety review, as big guns firm for Cox Plate and Caulfield Cup “We continued to grow addition revenue streams to support the club and reinvest in racing,” Fullarton said. MRC chairman Cameron Fisher said reducing debt remained the club board’s key priority, while the committee was committed to racing at Sandown. The club will hold its annual general meeting on Thursday night and will announce the results of its recent board elections during which 24-year-old newcomer Fergus Ewart stood against sitting members Caitrin Kelly, Belinda Meyers and Robyn Gray. title: Sad supermarket trend hitting Aussies at every income level: 'Nothing left to give'
text:
The cost of putting food on the table for Australian families is starting to sting, with new research revealing the growing pressure hitting household budgets.

As school holidays begin across much of Australia, families would normally be looking ahead to days out, activities and keeping the kids entertained.

But for a growing number of households, rising grocery costs are leaving little room in the budget for anything beyond the essentials. For others, the budget doesn't even stretch that far.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

New research by YouGov, commissioned by the St Vincent de Paul Society NSW, revealed that 83 per cent of Aussies are spending more on groceries than they were 12 months ago.

More than half, 55 per cent, said financial pressures have forced them to cut back on food purchases altogether.

All Australian income brackets are now feeling the cost-of-living pinch, with people saying they're spending more on groceries than a year ago, according to the study.

While those on higher incomes are better suited to weathering the storm, those less fortunate are increasingly turning to charities for help.

Food relief and homelessness charity Nourish Street founder Beau Haywood previously told Yahoo News that he is seeing more families and working Australians seeking support.

Food assistance accounted for 73 per cent of people assisted by Vinnies NSW over the past year. Source: Vinnies NSW/James Horan (James Horan)

The cost-of-living squeeze hits home

Financial pressures also made it harder for 55 per cent of survey respondents to keep their household stocked with essential items.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

The Society has seen a 5 per cent increase in requests for food assistance across NSW.

Yolanda Saiz, St Vincent de Paul Society NSW CEO, said the research reflects the cost-of-living reality many households are facing.

"A weekly grocery shop doesn't go as far as it used to. The price of almost everything has increased, but many household budgets simply haven't kept pace," said Saiz.

"It's heartbreaking to hear from parents who are skipping meals so their children can eat. No parent should have to make that choice, yet for many households it has become a reality.

"The survey shows Australians are buying less food because they simply can't afford the grocery bill, and we're seeing the consequences of that every day through increasing demand for food assistance."

The cost of filling a shopping trolley continues to climb for Australian families. Source: Getty Images (SOPA Images)

More than 100,000 people seek help

Over the past year, Vinnies NSW has assisted more than 106,000 people across the state, providing $9.7 million in food-related assistance through hampers, supermarket vouchers and Christmas hampers.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Food was one of the most common reasons people sought help, accounting for 73 per cent of those assisted by local members.

"Every day we are meeting with people who have already cut back everything they can. There is simply nothing left to give," Ms Saiz said.

"When households are buying less food and struggling to keep basic essentials stocked at home, it doesn't take much for a financial setback to become a crisis."

Vinnies NSW provided $9.7 million in food-related assistance to more than 106,000 people across the state over the past year. Source: Supplied

More Aussies reaching out for help

Vinnies NSW State President Peter Houweling said the organisation was continuing to rely on community support as demand increased.

"In cities and regional communities alike, we're seeing people who never imagined they would need assistance now reaching out for help with basic essentials," Houweling said.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"Our members and volunteers are helping families put food on the table, providing practical support and reminding people that they don't have to face these challenges alone."

Vinnies is now urging Australians who can afford to help to support its Hampers of Care appeal, with an $89 donation providing a household with essential food and grocery items.

"Making a donation is a small action that makes an immediate impact for someone in their time of need. Your donation means that someone will have food on the table tonight," Houweling added.

title: ‘Depressing’: Rebel’s box office flop
text:
There was a "beauty parade" of Australian distributors making offers for Rebel Wilson's directorial debut The Deb after it screened at the Toronto International Film Festival, a court has been told.

The NSW Supreme Court was told that production company AI Film was fielding four credible offers by November 2024 that suited the strategy for a successful Australian release and were a springboard for an extended international release.

However, the court was told that a defamation lawsuit in the US initiated by three producers of the film – Vince Holden, Gregor Cameron and Amanda Ghost – against Ms Wilson over an Instagram post she made was causing issues with some of the distributors to finalise the deal.

Rebel Wilson is accused of sabotaging her own film. Picture: NewsWire / John Appleyard

AI Film Production Ltd is suing Ms Wilson in the NSW Supreme Court, alleging she sabotaged and blocked the release of the film that was shot in Australia in late 2023.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She is accused of undermining negotiations with distributors and threatening legal action against anyone showing the movie.

AI Film also alleges she breached various contractual obligations and directorial duties, engaged in misleading or deceptive conduct and repeatedly committed the tort of injurious falsehood.

Mr Holden, Mr Cameron and Ms Ghost claim Wilson accused them in an Instagram post to her 11 million followers of inappropriate conduct towards the lead actor in the film, Charlotte MacInnes, embezzling funds and trying to block the film's release.

She has denied the allegations and filed a counter claim. Picture: NewsWire / John Appleyard

Ms Wilson has denied the allegations and filed a counter claim seeking almost $800,000 in production fees and costs she says is owed to her company Camp Sugar, which her mother Sue Bownds co-owns.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Ms Wilson and her mum sat side by side at the rear of the Sydney courtroom on Tuesday as Mr Holden continued his evidence about the distribution deals.

Eventually, Rialto secured the rights and proposed for the film to premiere in Australia on March 30, but it didn't happen until April 9, 2026.

The court was told it only made a little more than $300,000 at the box office, a figure Mr Holden described as "depressing".

The hearing continues.
